# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Children increasingly read machine-generated stories on screens, and whether the text properties governing laboratory reading also govern it there is unknown. We will analyse logs from *Let's Story*, in the *Applaydu* app, where children aged 7 and over read in any of 19 languages. Reading time per word will be modelled from word difficulty, grammatical load and how explicitly ideas are linked. Six confirmatory hypotheses concern these associations, their change with age, their selective weakening under narration, children's difficulty ratings and accumulated in-app reading. Each association, estimated with readings grouped by text, child and language, is judged against a pre-set smallest effect of interest. Associations clearly beyond it would support the hypotheses, in either direction for the two that separate rival developmental accounts, and those clearly below it would show that laboratory effects do not transfer. Because families choose narration, texts and continued use, every estimate is a conditional association.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Introduction

A generation of children now does part of its reading on a screen, and some of what appears there was written by a machine. In the United Kingdom, one in five 8- to 18-year-olds read fiction on screen at least monthly in 2025, and the share reading print fiction had fallen from three in five to one in two since 2017 [@pictonTrendsChildrenYoung2026]. The same report found that children reading fiction only on screen were disproportionately those who enjoyed reading least. Commercial storytelling applications generate a narrative to order, read it aloud in the family's language and record what the child did with it. One such feature reported 2.4 million story sessions in its first six months [@ratnerDidRobotWrite2025]. Yet many parents interviewed in one small study wanted the plot and dialogue of a child's story to remain human-authored, accepting machine-made illustrations only on that condition [@jinTheyAllLook2025]. The behavioural record such platforms accumulate far exceeds any laboratory corpus of children's reading, spans many languages and arises under the conditions that laboratory work excludes. We ask whether the text properties that govern reading under controlled conditions still govern it outside the laboratory, and whether their hold on the reader changes over the years in which decoding becomes automatic. Either answer bears on how far three determinants of reading established under experimental control extend to unsupervised reading, and on how their influence changes with age.

The laboratory findings are well established at three levels of linguistic description. In the Reading Systems Framework [@perfettiWordKnowledgeTheory2014], a word passes from identification through the lexicon to comprehension processes that include a parser, a text representation and a situation model. Within those processes, each word is integrated with the text read so far. This study's three text components, LexicalDifficulty, GrammaticalLoad and ReferentialContinuity, relate in turn to identifying words, parsing sentences and integrating each sentence with those before it. None of them measures the situation model a reader builds.

At the level of the word, high-frequency words are recognised faster and fixated for less time than low-frequency words, and frequency and word-length effects on text reading are closely similar across 12 alphabetic languages [@kupermanWordLengthFrequency2024a]. Those languages, including Greek and unpointed Hebrew, spell a word as a linear string of letters. @kupermanWordLengthFrequency2024a left out Korean, which stacks its letters into syllable blocks, because the distribution of its word lengths differed too much from the others'. Children's eye movements are driven by the frequency of the words they meet [@josephUsingEyeMovements2013]. Compared with adult controls, children showed larger length and frequency effects [@tiffin-richardsWordLengthFrequency2015], as predicted by an account on which the frequency effect tracks accumulated exposure [@brysbaertWordFrequencyEffect2018]. The same developmental pattern appears outside alphabetic scripts [@lianEffectsWordFrequency2026], and the Lexical Quality Hypothesis describes it [@perfettiReadingAbilityLexical2007; @perfettiWordKnowledgeTheory2014]. A word is retrieved quickly and reliably in proportion to how well specified and tightly bound its orthographic, phonological and semantic constituents are, and that quality is built by reading itself [@nationNurturingLexicalLegacy2017; @castlesEndingReadingWars2018]. On that account, a text's lexical properties, a child's age band (7 to 8, or 9 and over) and accumulated reading all bear on the cost of identifying a word. Hypothesis 1 tests the account through text properties, and Hypothesis 6 through accumulated in-app reading.

A second source of word-level cost is contextual. On surprisal theory, a word costs time in proportion to how unexpected it is given what precedes it [@haleProbabilisticEarleyParser2001; @levyExpectationbasedSyntacticComprehension2008]. The relation is close to linear in surprisal [@smithEffectWordPredictability2013; @shainLargescaleEvidenceLogarithmic2024] and holds in 11 languages from five families [@wilcoxTestingPredictionsSurprisal2023]. That linearity makes a text's mean per-word surprisal the natural text-level summary of the cost, and the design adopts it, allowing for two qualifications. A text's overall difficulty moderates how strongly per-word surprisal bears on reading time, so the text-level mean is not a neutral summary of a constant word-level effect [@chenTextDifficultyModulates2026]. Frequency and surprisal are hard to separate, since dissociable frequency effects shrink as surprisal predictors improve [@ohDissociableFrequencyEffects2025], which qualifies their reported additivity in naturalistic reading [@shainWordFrequencyPredictability2024]. LexicalDifficulty pools the two, so the confirmatory claim concerns their joint contribution and leaves the share of each unresolved. How subword tokens are aggregated to words affects psycholinguistic estimates [@giulianelliProperTreatmentTokenization2024], and the unit over which surprisal should be defined is being reconsidered [@kiegelandProperTreatmentUnits2026], so the aggregation rule is fixed under Materials. In children, contextual facilitation appears in the later eye-movement measures that a whole-text duration absorbs [@tiffinrichardsContextFacilitationText2020].

Further lexical properties enter the design, each for a different reason. Concrete words are fixated for less time than abstract ones in natural reading, on every fixation measure where length and frequency were matched [@yaoEmotionProcessingConcrete2024] and on first-fixation duration where they were covaried instead [@magnaboscoEyeSemanticsStudy2024]. That advantage is usually traced to perceptual grounding, on accounts that treat conceptual processing as partly modal and partly amodal [@kaupInterplayModalAmodal2025]. A word's age of acquisition bears on how quickly it is identified over and above its frequency [@juhaszAgeofacquisitionEffects2005]. Function words are skipped far more often than content words [@raynerEyeMovementsReading1998], so a text of higher lexical density (the proportion of content-word tokens) presents more tokens to be fixated and identified. Reading times for a word fall over repeated encounters, in children of 10 and 11 reading sentences [@josephExaminingIncidentalWord2018], so a lexical diversity index [@mccarthyMTLDVocdDHDD2010] tracks the share of tokens a reader meets for the first time. A word-level measure of informational cost predicts eye movements in first- and second-language readers of diverse writing systems [@kimchiQuantifyingWordInformativeness2025], though its authors test no text-level aggregate of the kind used here.

At the level of the sentence, structure imposes a further cost. Mean dependency distance indexes the distance over which a dependency must be resolved, and clause density, subordination and noun-phrase depth index how many dependencies are open at once. Structural cost is not reducible to predictability. In 368 adults reading syntactically challenging sentences, language-model surprisal from 409 estimators approximated the early effects of disambiguation but not the additional rereading that repairing a structure incurred [@timkeyEyeMovementsReveal2026]. For that reason, the grammatical features form a distinct family and are never absorbed into surprisal. Gibson's [-@gibsonLinguisticComplexityLocality1998] theory separates the cost of keeping a prediction alive from that of integrating the element that completes it. Retrieval-based accounts place the cost at the point of resolution, where intervening and similar material slows retrieval [@lewisActivationbasedModelSentence2005]. Expectation-based accounts add that the material before a head can make the head more predictable [@levyExpectationbasedSyntacticComprehension2008], so in head-final configurations a longer dependency need not cost more. A clause-final verb has been read faster after longer intervening material in German and Hindi [@koniecznyLocalityParsingComplexity2000; @vasishthArgumentheadDistanceProcessing2006], and the strength of a locality effect is expected to vary with a language's statistics [@futrellLossycontextSurprisalInformationtheoretic2020]. The grammatical slope is therefore allowed to vary by language in every model below.

Hypothesis 2 asks whether children bear these costs disproportionately. A prior question is whether a grammatical cost appears at all when reading time is measured over whole texts, as here. In naturalistic corpus reading by adults, a distance-based integration cost predicted reading times at nouns and auxiliaries but not at words in general, whereas word predictability predicted them throughout [@dembergDataEyetrackingCorpora2008]. In the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus, global measures of syntactic and lexical complexity (among them the longest dependency path, the proportion of embedded sentences and mean sentence length) predicted adults' passage reading negligibly once passage length was accounted for [@kupermanGlobalMeasuresSyntactic2025]. At the sentence level, that study found effects of any size only for sentence length and position. Its lexical measures proved as negligible as its syntactic ones, but its authors separate such global measures from the aggregate properties of a passage's individual words. LexicalDifficulty is anchored on those aggregates (mean frequency, word length and surprisal), whose word-level effects are well replicated across languages [@kupermanWordLengthFrequency2024a; @wilcoxTestingPredictionsSurprisal2023]. The grammatical question remains open for children reading whole stories, and Hypothesis 1 is framed so that either answer is informative.

At the level of the passage, the property of interest is whether the text states the connection between one idea and the next or leaves the reader to supply it. Sentence-to-sentence semantic similarity, overlap in referring expressions and the density of explicit connectives together index how much of that work the text's surface has already done [@crossleyToolAutomaticAnalysis2019]. These are measures of cohesion, a property of the text, whereas coherence is a property of the representation the reader builds, and cohesion eases its construction without guaranteeing it [@mcnamaraCohMetrixCapturingLinguistic2010]. Referential overlap descends from the rule that connects propositions sharing an argument [@kintschModelTextComprehension1978], which the construction-integration model retains in the weights it assigns to propositions close together in the text base [@kintschRoleKnowledgeDiscourse1988]. Semantic similarity between adjoining sentences approximates that propositional analysis [@foltzMeasurementTextualCoherence1998]. An explicit relational marker speeds processing of the segment it introduces without changing what is recalled [@sandersRoleCoherenceRelations2000]. Multi-dimensional characterisations of difficulty built from such indices outperform classical readability formulae [@crossleyAssessingReadabilityFormulas2023]. Evaluated against eye movements, though, readability scorers account for real-time reading ease only partially [@grutekekleinEyeTrackingBased2026]. Partly for that reason, this study models the psycholinguistic features and uses no composite readability score.

The systematic review accompanying this protocol refines these laboratory findings in ways that shape the design, and Supplementary Section S2 tabulates the studies closest to this study in method and modality. Text difficulty does not reduce to word frequency. In German fourth graders, estimated lexical coverage predicted comprehension non-linearly [@ludewigVocabularyTextCoverage2023]. In 158 children aged 8 to 11, word frequency, pronoun density, concreteness and deep cohesion each explained unique variance in passage comprehension once decoding and oral language were controlled, and lexical arousal explained variance beyond them [@pickrenContributionTextCharacteristics2022]. That result warrants including affective and discourse variables alongside conventional readability measures. Syntactic complexity impaired comprehension accuracy and slowed recall in bilingual children [@wasitokiranaSentenceProcessingIndonesianEnglish2025]. In 5,133 second graders reading informational text, word concreteness, referential cohesion and deep cohesion each predicted oral reading rate beyond classical readability formulae [@tortorelliBeyondFirstGrade2020]. In 78 first graders, the mean log frequency of a text's words predicted reading accuracy, words correct per minute and maze comprehension [@brunerRoleTextVocabulary2026]. Both samples read aloud and fall within or below this study's younger band. They establish the association with oral reading rate, without fixing its size among children of 9 and over, or in the app, where a child may read silently, aloud or along with narration.

Two further strands concern the reader and the reading context. On the reader's side, longitudinal work shows that a child's reading history is not a simple quantity of practice. In random-intercept cross-lagged models from ages 7 to 16, weaker early reading predicted less subsequent leisure reading, while later within-person increases in book reading predicted gains in comprehension [@torppaLeisureReadingNot2020]. A 10-year study likewise found reciprocal associations between skill and print exposure, with the skill-to-practice path most visible early and accumulated exposure more predictive later [@vanbergenHowArePractice2021]. Accumulated use of an app reflects both practice and the stable differences in skill and motivation that produced the use, so Hypothesis 6 separates within-child change from between-child differences. The setting matters as well as the quantity. Digital leisure reading and print reading do not relate to comprehension in the same way [@altamuraNewFormsReading2025], and digital leisure reading is associated with comprehension independently of print [@altamuraHowDigitalReading2025]. Hypothesis 6 counts only reading inside one app.

As for the reading context, read-aloud narration is often treated as a uniform benefit, but the evidence does not support that view. A meta-analysis of 30 reading-while-listening studies, 62 effects over a total *N* of 1,945, found a small pooled comprehension advantage (*g* = 0.18). There was no reliable advantage where ordinary reading was self-paced (*g* = 0.06, 95 per cent CI [-0.07, 0.19]), and a larger one only where the experimenter paced it (*g* = 0.41, 95 per cent CI [0.13, 0.70]) [@clintonlisellDoesReadingWhile2023]. Among students with reading difficulties, text-to-speech tools showed a moderate pooled effect (*d* = 0.35) that fell to *d* = 0.15, with an interval including zero, in within-participant designs [@woodUseTexttoSpeech2018]. Neither synthesis identifies the mechanism, which a large naturalistic corpus is well placed to address. A spoken rendition may work by supplying word identity, in which case it should remove much of the cost of lexical difficulty while leaving the cost of connecting ideas intact. Alternatively, the audio's duration may set narrated reading time. Hypothesis 4 is designed to distinguish these decoding-scaffolding and audio-pacing accounts.

The generated stories studied here are a population of stimuli produced by one process, and a process need not distribute text properties as human authorship does. Comparisons in other domains report that large-language-model output has a distinct noun-heavy, informationally dense register even when prompted otherwise [@reinhartLLMsWriteHumans2025]. Human writing in those comparisons shows more scattered sentence-length distributions and more varied vocabulary than model output [@munoz-ortizContrastingLinguisticPatterns2024]. In creative writing, the domain closest to these stories, stylometric comparison separates the two on measurable features of style [@osullivanStylometricComparisonsHuman2025]. Whether the lexical, grammatical and discourse determinants established on human-written text describe reading across such a population is a question about the scope of those findings [@haeffelTestsGeneralizabilityCan2022; @yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2022].

To gauge how much published work combines this study's topics, we searched Scopus on 26 August 2026 for records from 2018 onwards. The search returned 3,701 records on children's reading comprehension, 6,592 on computational text features and 133,132 on platform log data. The pairwise intersections were 17, 28 and 45 records, and the three-way intersection was empty. The search covered one database under one set of expressions and missed the log analysis of this platform described below, although it had appeared two months earlier. The empty cell shows only that the intersection is thin and unevenly indexed, not that it is unoccupied. @fig-gap shows the sets, and Supplementary Section S4 records the search expressions and the publication trend. The search script, which archives the counts, is deposited with this protocol [@bernabeuScopusflow2026].

Over the same window, records combining children's reading with machine-generated text went from none before 2024 to two in 2024, six in 2025 and four in the first eight months of 2026. The studies are classroom experiments that report gains in comprehension and motivation but describe the texts only qualitatively [@balantekinImprovingStudentsReading2026; @bulutImpactAISTEMBased2026]. Generated and human-written texts have been compared directly, though not yet in children reading for themselves. Generated stories had fewer personal pronouns and more positive emotion than 100 human-written ones, and adult readers were less transported by them [@appelChatGPTLinguisticProperties2025]. The models tested for children's stories could not hold their vocabulary to a level appropriate for younger readers [@valentiniAutomaticGenerationSimplification2023], a limitation that bears directly on the lexical component.

*Let's Story*, a feature of the *Applaydu* app developed by Gameloft and Ferrero International, combines the three topics of the Scopus search. Children choose a hero, a companion, a setting, a plot and a theme, as the session table records (Supplementary Section S8), and a generative model writes a narrative around those choices [@ratnerDidRobotWrite2025]. The app presents the narrative as an illustrated storybook, reads it aloud at the family's option [@ratnerDidRobotWrite2025] and logs every completed reading. Comparable platforms have been studied one feature at a time. @bootonImpactMobileApplication2023 reviewed 11 studies and found inbuilt narration to aid comprehension and word learning. Log data from a research-oriented platform track ability, with reading speed in the BookBites app correlating with standardised scores at *r* = .39 to .48 [@sortkaerBothSidesStory2021]. The commercial edutainment sector, with a far larger audience, is described in the literature we identified mainly by content analyses and small experiments [@furlongFindingNeedleHaystack2025; @chatzopoulosEvaluationGooglePlay2023].

One analysis of logs from *Let's Story* itself has been published. Over 419,700 story sessions in 18 languages across the 30 days following the feature's launch in November 2024, @ratnerProductiveStruggleChildrens2026 describe how children aged 4 to 9 meet challenge. They report completion, the post-reading difficulty rating and where in a story abandoned sessions stopped. The analysis is descriptive by design and drawn from aggregated dashboard counts, so its authors state that it cannot follow an individual reader. Because it models no reading time and its summaries lacked the session-level structure a within-child term requires, it leaves every association registered here untested. Its window was the first month after launch, whereas ours opens more than a year later, so the novelty effects its authors mention apply much less here. The study does establish that the difficulty rating, the completion requirement and the session record can be analysed in large samples on this platform.

The theoretical commitments behind the hypotheses are set out in a machine-checkable theory object deposited with this protocol. It names twelve constructs, eighteen propositions, six auxiliary assumptions and six rival accounts. Each proposition states its mechanism, and each of the ten predictions is recorded with the proposition it derives from and, for seven, the rival it is diagnostic against. The object claims that the time a child spends per word is set by the costs a text imposes at the word, the sentence and the passage. Three reader capacities reduce those costs: the automaticity of print-to-sound mapping, verbal working memory and the readiness to supply an unstated connection. A spoken rendition bears more on the first than on the third. The platform records none of the three, and the age band stands in for them. Five further propositions extend the same constructs to the quality of the mental model a child ends with. They could be examined only in exploratory analyses at Stage 2, and only if comprehension items prove to exist, as set out under Contingent hypotheses. @fig-net, generated from the object, draws its constructs and the paths between them. The object satisfies all twelve items of the versioned rigour checklist in theoryforge, scoring 90.7 out of 100 (Supplementary Section S1) [@bernabeuTheoryforge2026]. Its causal graph is acyclic, so the independence claims it entails can be derived formally. Before interpreting the confirmatory models, we will test three of them, listed with their criterion under Outcome-neutral quality checks, and report any failure.

This study is observational throughout. Families choose the stories, the reading level and whether narration is on, and decide whether to keep using the app. A laboratory experiment establishes that a text property can change reading when an experimenter controls the text, the setting and the task. The further question, whether the property does so when nothing is controlled, concerns generalisation and cannot be answered in the setting that produced the original result [@yarkoniGeneralizabilityCrisis2022; @nastaseKeepItReal2020]. Whether a relation holds in a new population of texts, languages and readers therefore tests the account that predicts it [@haeffelTestsGeneralizabilityCan2022]. In the logs of a vocabulary-learning app, a laboratory effect of valence held whereas one of concreteness did not [@wildWordLearningWild2024], though those users were adults and the outcome was learning.

The platform offers three gains in return for that loss of control, beginning with stimulus sampling. Reading research has known since Clark [-@clarkLanguageasfixedeffectFallacy1973] that treating a handful of experimenter-written texts as a fixed set inflates confidence in conclusions meant to hold for texts in general. The mixed-model solution has been available for over a decade [@juddTreatingStimuliRandom2012]. The design treats Text as a crossed random factor over hundreds of texts that families selected, which is both the prescribed remedy and, in Brunswik's sense, a representative design [@dhamiRoleRepresentativeDesign2004]. A varying intercept does not by itself make an inference general where the variation between texts is systematic [@bearRandomEffectsWont2022], so the model includes the systematic sources of variation the platform records. Because an average over texts can hide the variation between them [@simonsohnStimulusSamplingReimagined2025], the text-level deviations will be displayed against the component scores at Stage 2. We avoid the phrase *ecological validity*, used in at least two senses, Brunswik's and Orne's [@kihlstromEcologicalValidityEcological2021], and argued to be too ill-defined to bear on generalisation [@hollemanRealWorldApproachIts2020]. Our claim is the narrower, checkable one about how the stimuli were sampled.

The second gain, linguistic breadth, matters because English dominates cognitive science to a degree that warps which mechanisms are studied and licenses overgeneralisation from one atypical language to the species [@blasiOverrelianceEnglishHinders2022]. Reading is among the worst affected, because writing systems differ in ways that matter for every stage of processing. The most ambitious response to date, the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus, assembled eye-tracking during text reading in 13 languages, since extended to 21 [@siegelmanExpandingHorizonsCrosslinguistic2022; @siegelmanWave2Multilingual2025]. Its authors report that the existing empirical base is insufficient for cross-linguistic comparison. A commercial platform covers many of the same languages incidentally, with far more readers per language, and its readers are children, whereas the corpus records skilled adults. The platform records only whole-story durations, so it gains breadth at the cost of the resolution an eye-movement record gives.

The lexical and continuity associations are expected in their predicted directions in every language the extract contains. The app offers 19: Arabic, Dutch, English, French, German, Greek, Hebrew, Indonesian, Italian, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, Simplified Chinese, Spanish, Thai, Traditional Chinese and Turkish. The operations reading recruits, mapping a written form to sound and to meaning and relating it to what came before, are common to writing systems that differ in almost everything else [@frostUniversalModelReading2012; @verhoevenUniversalsLearningRead2022]. The cross-linguistic evidence reviewed above bears this out for the lexical properties in alphabetic scripts and in Chinese, although it leaves out Korean and Thai. Averaged over languages, the grammatical association is expected in its predicted direction, but expectation-based accounts allow it to weaken or vanish in head-final structures, as in German and Dutch verb-final clauses and throughout Korean and Turkish. Because head-final languages also minimise dependency length much less than head-initial ones [@futrellLargeScaleEvidence2015], the grammatical association should vary most across languages. The lexical association should vary in magnitude with how a script encodes the word, most of all where it departs from a linear string of letters separated by spaces. Korean stacks its letters into syllable blocks, Chinese characters stand for syllables and morphemes, Chinese and Thai leave the boundaries between words unmarked, and Arabic and Hebrew usually leave short vowels unwritten. Orthographic depth may add further differences among the alphabetic languages, since children's length and frequency effects are orthography-specific even where adults' converge [@schroederEyeMovementsChildren2022]. No comparable reason has been derived for referential continuity, which operates above the word. These expectations concern the language-varying component slopes, reported for every language, though no verdict in @tbl-design rests on any one of them.

The third gain is behaviour logged by the app as it occurred. Logged and self-reported digital media use diverge systematically enough to have warranted a meta-analysis of the discrepancy [@parrySystematicReviewMetaanalysis2021]. Among 109 French primary-school children, parents' estimates of weekly reading time were three times the logged figure, which predicted fluency better [@brossetteMeasuringReadingTime2026].

Against these gains stands the strongest statistical objection to any large non-random dataset. Meng's [-@mengStatisticalParadisesParadoxes2018] decomposition shows that the error of a sample mean is the product of three quantities: data quality, data quantity and the difficulty of the problem. Data quality is the correlation between the recorded value and whether it was recorded at all, and probability sampling keeps it near zero. Once it is no longer near zero, the population size stops cancelling, and estimation error grows with the square root of the population for any given sample size. Bradley and colleagues [-@bradleyUnrepresentativeBigSurveys2021] gave the canonical demonstration. Two surveys collecting about 250,000 responses a week and 75,000 a fortnight overestimated United States COVID-19 vaccine uptake by 17 and 14 percentage points, with margins of error so small that the wrong answers looked precise. A well-designed panel of about 1,000 responses a week, by contrast, was accurate. Every point of selection here is a candidate for that correlation: who owns a tablet, who installs an app tied to a confectionery brand, who registers consent for research use, who switches narration off and who finishes a story.

Meng's result, however, concerns the estimation of a population mean, and this study estimates none. Its estimands are conditional associations inside the sample, within a language and within a reading level. A point of selection that depends on the reader alone, such as who owns a tablet or who registers consent, changes which children a slope describes without distorting it. Where the reader attribute also moderates the slope, the estimate becomes the average slope across the families who use the platform. An estimate of a heterogeneous association from a non-random sample should be interpreted as such an average [@bryanBehaviouralScienceUnlikely2021]. We will report these coefficients as estimates for children who read on this platform, never as population values for children in general, and will report no population mean of reading speed for any group. A slope is distorted only when selection is a common effect of the text property, or of something correlated with it, and of the outcome or of an unmeasured cause of the outcome [@hernanStructuralApproachSelection2004; @elwertEndogenousSelectionBias2014; @lampCorrectingColliderEffects2025]. That condition is narrower than the one that biases a mean. Of the points of selection listed above, only completion meets it. Narration is a state the models condition on, so the selection it involves affects the denominators of the Hypothesis 4 proportions and is addressed with that hypothesis.

The extract that the app's data controller will transfer contains completed readings only, so the analysis conditions on completion, which is plausibly a common effect of the text's difficulty and the reader's capacity. Conditioning on a common effect can induce an association between its causes where none existed [@rohrerThinkingClearlyCorrelations2018], and the direction here is predictable. If harder texts are abandoned more often, the hard texts that remain are disproportionately those read by children who could manage them, which attenuates the coefficients Hypothesis 1 predicts. If younger children abandon demanding texts more often, their remaining readings of such texts are the more selected and their slopes the more attenuated [@elwertEndogenousSelectionBias2014; @hernanSelectionBiasDue2023]. On the sign convention given below, that attenuation pushes the grammatical interaction positive and the continuity interaction negative, towards the bottleneck-release and cue-utilisation accounts of Hypotheses 2 and 3 respectively. The bias therefore works against our predictions, so a non-negligible result withstands the objection better than a null does. Where the data controller can supply the completion rate by age band, we will report it with every verdict on Hypotheses 1 to 3. If the younger band's rate is the lower, a verdict supporting the bottleneck-release or cue-utilisation account will be reported as also consistent with differential attrition.

A reader can cope with a demanding text without abandoning it, by reading it less carefully. When reading speed was manipulated, comprehension held across a broad range of rates and fell only at the fastest, around 405 words per minute, while the influence of word properties on eye movements persisted throughout [@schwalmTestingSpeedaccuracyTradeoff2026]. That result places the 400-words-per-minute plausibility bound close to the rate at which comprehension gave way, so the bound removes page-flipping but keeps fast, still comprehending reading. The same study gives no warrant for assuming that faster readings show weaker text effects, since its word-level effects did not weaken with speed. Neither the extract nor the design can separate a skimmed reading from a fluent one, so we register the ambiguity without assigning it a direction.

We do not use causal verbs for variables that families chose. The questions are nonetheless causal, and we say so because euphemism has been argued to damage observational research by obscuring what is being asked [@hernanCWordScientificEuphemisms2018; @groszTabooAgainstExplicit2020]. We state the causal structure in the theory object's causal graph, derive the adjustment set from it, register the rival explanations it implies and report associations conditional on that adjustment.

Secondary data invite the analytic flexibility that preregistration exists to remove, and the field has standards for preregistering analyses of existing data [@westonRecommendationsIncreasingTransparency2019; @vandenakkerPreregistrationSecondaryData2021]. The arrangement described under Data provenance goes further, since the data controller holds the extract, unanalysed, and will transfer it only after in-principle acceptance. As a result, the most common objection to observational work, that the analyst saw the data before choosing the analysis, does not arise. Withholding the outcome until the analysis is fixed is the principle of blind analysis [@maccounBlindAnalysisHide2015; @dutilhFlexibleYetFair2021].

The analysis estimates a few pre-specified associations and does not attempt to predict an individual child's reading. We calculated the precision attainable for each without access to the extract and state in advance which of them the available records cannot resolve. Group-level associations need not describe any individual, since variance around an expected value was two to four times larger within people than within groups [@fisherLackGrouptoindividualGeneralizability2018]. The within-child analysis uses tier 2, the user accounts with at least three eligible readings of distinct texts, to separate each child's own change from differences between children. The two are never reported as a single quantity.

The design allows for three features of the platform and its records. First, the reading level a family sets determines which version of a text the platform presents, so text difficulty is partly assigned by a choice that also reflects the child's capacity. We will estimate the text coefficients within reading level and check whether they persist under that restriction. Second, the outcome is a whole-story rate, and we state below what such a rate can and cannot index. Third, the data contain no measure of a child's reading skill, vocabulary or language background. The reading language a family selects need not be the child's first language, so every coefficient below averages over children reading in a first and in a second language. In adult bilinguals reading paragraphs, frequency effects were larger in the second language than in the first and grew as second-language exposure fell [@whitfordSecondlanguageExperienceModulates2012]. A reading language is not a language background, and the country-by-language analysis registered under Sensitivity analyses is the extract's only means of addressing the difference. Without measures of skill and vocabulary, the age band stands in for a bundle of developing capacities.

Accounts of reading development suggest what the age band can index when no measure of skill is available. Under the simple view, reading comprehension is the product of decoding and language comprehension, and decoding's share of the variance falls across the primary grades [@goughDecodingReadingReading1986; @hooverSimpleViewReading1990; @loniganExaminingSimpleView2018]. On automaticity theory, that share falls because identification that runs without deliberate attention releases capacity for integration [@labergeTowardTheoryAutomatic1974; @perfettiReadingAbilityLexical2007]. Phonological recoding on each new word is the mechanism by which reading itself produces that automaticity [@sharePhonologicalRecodingSelfteaching1995], which ties Hypothesis 6 to that theory. In a longitudinal eye-movement study, reading efficiency rose by 36 per cent between grades 2 and 4, and linguistic skill determined the change whereas oculomotor skill did not [@huesteggeOculomotorLinguisticDeterminants2009]. Among 194 Greek-speaking children, silent reading speed rose from 111 words per minute in grade 3 to 166 in grade 6, through fewer and shorter fixations and longer saccades [@gleniContributionEyeMovements2026]. In the same study, those oculomotor parameters explained variance in speed beyond vocabulary and cognitive measures. The age band is therefore interpreted as a coarse, aggregate proxy for reading experience and the automaticity it confers, not for any single capacity.

The platform sets the boundary between the age bands. It describes its audience as children of 4 to 9 [@ratnerProductiveStruggleChildrens2026], so the older band is expected to lie mostly at its lower edge, and its upper edge is not recorded. Whether change across such a boundary is governed by attained reading level or maturing oculomotor control is still debated [@justinoEyeMovementsDuring2023; @louwenEyeMovementsNatural2026]. These data can address that question only through the finer-age sensitivity analysis registered below.

Every hypothesis but Hypothesis 5 has the same outcome, the time a child spends per word over a whole story. In the laboratory, reading time is informative about processing because a word is fixated for about as long as it takes to process [@justTheoryReadingEye1980]. The properties that lengthen fixations predict passage-level eye-movement measures on texts of more than 200 words, a relation shown so far in second-language readers of English [@nahatameRevisitingTextReadability2025]. The theory object records this inference as the auxiliary assumption that elapsed time indexes effort, on which six of its ten predictions depend. The positive control on recorded reading time, registered under Outcome-neutral quality checks, puts that assumption at risk. A whole-text rate is more than the sum of its word-level costs, since the efficiency of processing items in a series explained variance in reading connected text once discrete word reading was controlled [@romeroBeyondWordRecognition2024]. The components are properties of the text, so differences in readers' efficiency are absorbed by the age band, the residual and, where it is fitted, the Account intercept. We describe the outcome as reading pace, an index of the processing demand a text imposes, and not as a measure of comprehension or fluency, because nothing in these data supports either description.

The theory object registers one rival interpretation of the outcome, the engagement account. It traces time on a story to how engaging the story is, whereas this study traces it to how demanding the text is. Among 122 sixth graders reading silently, passage difficulty, rated situational interest and their interaction all predicted time on task, and interest accounted for the most variance [@wellandEffectsReadingInstructional2025]. Two registered predictions are marked diagnostic against the engagement account. For the continuity coefficient, that account would produce a non-negligible positive value, since a text that states more of its connections might hold a child longer. The theory predicts instead that such a text should let the child finish sooner. Hypothesis 5 is also diagnostic, because a difficulty rating formed from effort the child noticed expending should rank the three components as reading time does, but a rating tracking enjoyment need not. Neither prediction alone rules out the engagement account.

Two of the six confirmatory hypotheses below concern interactions between a text property and the age band. Both are registered as two-sided tests that adjudicate between rival accounts, because the direct developmental evidence in this age range supports neither sign.

The age band and narration enter the models as deviations from their observed prevalence in tier 1 (the first eligible reading of each text by each user account). A reading scores 1 for the older band, or for narration on, and 0 otherwise, minus the proportion of tier-1 readings in that state. Each component's main effect is then its prevalence-weighted average slope across the two states, free of design effects from imbalance. Each interaction is the difference in slope between the two states, positive when the slope is larger in the older band or under narration. The reading-time outcome is log-transformed and standardised within language, so a coefficient is a within-language standardised slope. The region of practical equivalence, the range of effects treated as negligible, has a half-width of 0.05 standard deviations for such a slope. Hypothesis 4 concerns a difference between two attenuation proportions, with a region of half-width 0.05 on that difference. Hypothesis 5 uses the child's own three-point difficulty rating, and its region has a half-width of log(1.05) on the log-odds scale, corresponding to odds ratios between 0.952 and 1.05.

LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad are oriented so that higher scores mean a more demanding text, and ReferentialContinuity so that higher scores mean a text that states more of the links between its ideas. The orientations are fixed before any component score is linked to outcome data. Because the main effects of grammatical load and referential continuity run in opposite directions, the same developmental claim takes opposite signs in the two interactions. Grammatical load is associated with slower reading, so a weaker association in older children makes a positive slope smaller and the interaction negative. Referential continuity is associated with faster reading, so a weaker association in older children makes a negative slope less negative and the interaction positive.

Children in the two age bands differ in overall reading rate, and a purely multiplicative difference in rate produces a spurious interaction on a raw time scale [@faustIndividualDifferencesInformation1999]. On the log scale, such a difference appears only as a main effect, so every interaction reported here is a difference in *proportional* cost.

The log transformation leaves two other sources of interaction in place. First, an interaction can arise from an additive component of the interval. If the time a word costs is a base decoding time plus a grammatical increment, the log-scale grammatical slope is that increment divided by the base. A reader with a smaller base then shows a larger proportional slope even when the increment is identical. The bottleneck-release account posits an additive decoding component of this kind, so a positive Hypothesis 2 interaction is that account's expected signature on this scale, not an artefact of the transformation. Second, part of any whole-story interval is spent on the illustrations, on turning pages and away from the task. Children's attention to the text of an illustrated book rises across the primary grades [@roycharlandEyeMovementsShared2007], so the non-reading share may be larger in the younger band. The younger band's proportional slopes would then be smaller, moving the Hypothesis 2 interaction towards the positive sign and the Hypothesis 3 interaction towards the negative one. No registered test decides whether a smaller base interval reflects faster decoding or less time away from the text, although the lexical interaction below and the page-count refit under Sensitivity analyses bear on it. A practically non-negligible interaction of either sign will be reported with that limitation.

The remaining age-band interaction, LexicalDifficulty × AgeBand, has no registered test, and the theory object's propositions assign it no sign. The bottleneck-release account, which the theory object registers as a rival, nonetheless predicts a negative or null interaction, for reasons set out with Hypothesis 3. The eye-movement literature establishes larger absolute lexical effects in children [@tiffin-richardsWordLengthFrequency2015] without showing whether they are larger as a proportion of a slower baseline, the quantity a log outcome measures. The developmental evidence comes from raw latencies on isolated words. Across grades 2 to 4, word length and regularity effects declined while frequency effects persisted [@hessSublexicalLexicalProcessing2026]. In Italian children of grades 1 to 3, sensitivity to word length fell with age, in a study that manipulated length alone [@zoccolottiWordLengthEffect2005].

Expressing the outcome per word addresses one confound and leaves another. In the standard cohesion manipulation, the more cohesive version of a text is 20 to 40 per cent longer. A whole-text duration would then show higher cohesion slowing reading for arithmetic reasons alone. Dividing by word count and retaining log text length as a covariate closes that path, and a raw duration is never used as an outcome. A per-word rate still includes the extra time readers spend at sentence boundaries, time whose cause is uncertain [@raynerEffectClauseWrapup2000; @warrenInvestigatingCausesWrapup2009], and a text of shorter sentences has more boundaries per word. The boundary time works against the expected sign of sentence length taken alone.

@tbl-design sets out each hypothesis against the sampling and analysis plan that tests it, the precision the design analysis calls for, how each possible outcome will be interpreted and what would be shown wrong. We fixed every row before we had any access to outcome data.
