*Hypothesis 1: text properties and reading pace.* We predict that, across distinct texts and within reading level and language, LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad will each be positively associated with log reading time per word, and ReferentialContinuity negatively. The three coefficients are evaluated and labelled separately under the interpretations in @tbl-design, and the failure of one does not suppress reporting of the others. A positive continuity coefficient is not labelled a reverse cohesion effect, because that effect is a learning outcome [@mcnamaraAreGoodTexts1996; @mcnamaraLearningTextsEffects1996; @oreillyReversingCohesionEffect2007]. On the construction-integration model, the effect arises when a less cohesive text makes the knowledgeable reader infer more. The extra inference would appear on a time scale as slower reading of that text, in the predicted direction. A grammatical coefficient practically equivalent to zero would extend to children the negligible passage-level effect of global complexity measures reported for adults [@kupermanGlobalMeasuresSyntactic2025]. That interpretation does not apply to the lexical component, whose anchors are word-level aggregates the adult study did not test at passage level.

The narration rule follows from how narration is distributed. Narration was on in about nine sessions in ten of the structural sample, so each prevalence-weighted main effect is dominated by the narrated slope. If the audio sets the pace of narrated sessions, the narrated continuity slope converges on zero and the lexical slope on the slope of audio duration per word, as explained under Hypothesis 4. The compression diagnostic, the ratio of the narrated to the unnarrated residual standard deviation, signals such pacing when it falls below the cut-off registered under Confirmatory models. Where the diagnostic indicates compression and the distinct texts with unnarrated readings meet a component's threshold, that component's Hypothesis 1 verdict rests on the derived unnarrated slope, with the prevalence-weighted slope also reported. Each component's threshold is set by the seventh adjustment registered under Design and precision analysis. If compression is indicated but the texts with unnarrated readings fall short of that threshold, the prevalence-weighted verdict is retained and reported alongside the unnarrated slope. In that case, an inside-region continuity verdict or a non-negligible lexical verdict is reported as consistent with the audio having set the pace. The rule does not depend on the sign of any coefficient.

*Hypothesis 2: grammatical load and the age band.* We register the GrammaticalLoad × AgeBand interaction as a two-sided adjudicating test, because developmental accounts predict opposite signs on this study's scale. On the capacity account, formulated for individual differences among adults, a grammatical dependency costs time in proportion to how close its maintenance comes to exhausting the working memory available [@justCapacityTheoryComprehension1992; @kingIndividualDifferencesSyntactic1991]. Our developmental extension predicts a negative interaction, because working-memory capacity grows steadily across the primary-school years [@gathercoleStructureWorkingMemory2004] and the same structure should then cost the older reader proportionally less. Consistent with that extension, span measures in a cross-sectional sample of French-speaking children of 5 to 12 predicted complex-syntax comprehension, repetition and production over and above age [@delageSyntaxWorkingMemory2019]. The experience account predicts the same sign but attributes the change with age to growing exposure to complex structure, since exposure makes such structure cheaper [@macdonaldReassessingWorkingMemory2002]. Evidence that children with more print exposure produce relative clauses more as adults do [@montagInfluenceLanguageStatistics2015] concerns production, not the cost of reading such a structure.

The bottleneck-release account predicts the opposite sign, locating the change with age in the base over which the proportion is taken and in how fully structure is built on that base. As print-to-sound mapping automatises, the base decoding time shrinks [@labergeTowardTheoryAutomatic1974], leaving the reader with representations whose quality makes retrieval cheap [@perfettiReadingAbilityLexical2007]. An unchanged absolute grammatical cost then occupies a larger proportion of a smaller base, and the interaction is positive. As for how fully structure is built, comprehenders often leave syntactic structure shallow or unresolved [@ferreiraGoodEnoughRepresentations2002], although the evidence for such shallow processing is mixed [@francesGoodEnoughProcessing2024]. Globally ambiguous relative-clause attachments are read faster than disambiguated ones when readers expect only superficial questions [@swetsUnderspecificationSyntacticAmbiguities2008], an advantage that may owe more to reanalysing the disambiguated versions than to leaving structure unresolved [@staubAmbiguityAdvantageEffect2026]. Reading in the app resembles that low-demand condition, since the app, as far as the data controller has disclosed, asks children nothing about a story's content, which question (m) in @tbl-unresolved asks it to confirm. Children of 8 to 10 show the same signatures of shallow processing as adults, and the older among them attend more to the punctuation that marks clause boundaries [@wonnacottChildrensReadingGood2016]. On this view, a younger reader who builds shallower structure incurs less of a dependency's cost. In its developmental form, the capacity account is the theory object's own proposition, and the bottleneck-release account is registered there as its rival. A positive interaction would therefore count both against that proposition and for the rival.

The premise of our developmental extension, that working memory limits the processing of complex syntax, is less secure in this age range than the adult evidence suggests. Across 197 studies, the relation between working memory and reading was moderate, *r* = .29, and its contribution to comprehension was accounted for by decoding and vocabulary where those were controlled [@pengExaminingMediationEffects2018]. For relative-clause comprehension, the link was narrow in both studies we identified. In German-speaking 7-year-olds, the relation was to digit span and held for object relatives alone [@arosioMorphologicalInformationMemory2012], and in French- and German-speaking children, verbal working memory correlated with object-relative comprehension only in French [@solaimaniBilingualismWorkingMemory2025]. The only study we found that related span to online processing in children ran against the capacity account. Among 250 children of 8 to 11 reading and hearing sentences word by word, those with high digit spans slowed more than those with low spans on entering a relative clause [@boothDevelopmentRelativeClause2000]. Partly because the premise may not hold uniformly across the languages in this sample, the interaction is also reported separately by language.

The direct evidence does not decide between the accounts. The largest eye-movement study at these ages, with 81 children reading 12 items, found no attenuation [@wonnacottChildrensReadingGood2016]. It manipulated temporary ambiguity, which indexes reanalysis, a different demand from the sustained maintenance that dependency length imposes, so its null result does not transfer to the present operationalisation. Where an interaction has been reported, it was confined to late measures, in a study with 14 children per group [@josephChildrensAdultsOnline2013]. Recomputed from that study's tables as a proportion of baseline, the effects on two of its measures disagree. On go-past time in the target region, our computation gives 15 per cent in the younger children, 25 per cent in the older and 31 per cent in adults. That rise with age is the pattern a positive interaction would produce on a proportional scale. On post-target total reading time, where the study's own significant interaction lay, the proportional effect ran the other way. It was 27 per cent in the younger children, 12 per cent in the older and 4.5 per cent in adults.

A third possibility is that development across these ages is not monotonic. The study of 250 children, the largest existing test, also reported a U-shaped developmental pattern in the online processing of restrictive relative clauses [@boothDevelopmentRelativeClause2000]. Offline comprehension of complex syntax grows most steeply between 5;6 and 7 years [@frizelleDevelopmentRelativeClause2025], so the younger band falls immediately after the steepest phase. Online processing, however, can go on changing after accuracy has converged. In a spoken sentence-picture matching task with 16 children per age group, Russian-speaking children of 6 to 7 were less accurate than those of 8 to 10 and adults on every sentence type [@kruchininaEyemovementSignaturesSyntactic2026]. Unlike adults, they showed at most a partial eye-movement signature of revision at the passive participle. Children of 8 to 10 matched adults on accuracy and showed the adults' signature, yet still fixated the target picture less often while hearing the verb. An age difference that accuracy no longer registers may therefore persist in reading pace.

@tbl-design interprets each Hypothesis 2 outcome and states two caveats on a posterior inside the region.

*Hypothesis 3: referential continuity and the age band.* We register the ReferentialContinuity × AgeBand interaction as a second two-sided adjudicating test, because theory supplies two moderators of coherence facilitation that push the interaction in opposite directions. They are background knowledge and knowledge of the cue, each rising between 7 and 11. The first derives from the construction-integration model [@kintschRoleKnowledgeDiscourse1988], and the second from what exploiting a cohesive cue requires. On the knowledge account, a gap in the text is bridged from knowledge that the younger reader has less of and retrieves less readily. Age differences in coherence inferencing between 6 and 15 persisted when the relevant knowledge was made equally available to every child, and its accessibility mattered more for younger children [@barnesEffectsKnowledgeAvailability1996]. At 11 to 12, higher knowledge went with faster reading of sentences that required an inference [@cainInfluenceReaderText2024]. Surface continuity substitutes for an inference that is costlier at 7 to 8 than at 9 and over, so it is worth more to the younger reader and the interaction is positive.

On the cue-utilisation account, exploiting a connective requires enough decoding fluency to reach it and enough explicit knowledge of what it signals, so the older reader gains more and the interaction is negative. Knowledge of causal and adversative conjunctions is still developing between 8 and 10 [@cainAgeAbilityrelatedDifferences2005; @cainInfluenceConnectivesYoung2011], and comprehension of connectives grows across the primary years [@volodinaComprehensionConnectivesDevelopment2020]. Like the capacity account, the knowledge account is the theory object's own proposition, with the cue-utilisation account registered there as its rival, so a negative interaction would count against that proposition.

The cue-utilisation account depends on decoding fluency, so it implies a larger negative interaction where decoding is still maturing across the two bands, which the orthographic-depth paragraph below places in English, French and Portuguese. The knowledge account, resting on background knowledge and narrative experience, implies no such dependence. The per-language interactions registered under Sensitivity analyses are reported partly for that reason.

Decoding fluency and knowledge of the cue develop well past the ages studied here. Knowledge of what a connective signals is still incomplete in French-speaking teenagers of 12 to 19 and native Russian-speaking teenagers of 11 to 17. In both samples, vocabulary size and exposure to print were stronger correlates of appropriate use than age [@tskhovrebovaFrenchspeakingTeenagersMastery2022; @tskhovrebovaVocabularySizeExposure2023]. Both moderators are likely to grow with the reading a child accumulates, a further reason the net sign of the interaction cannot be derived in advance.

The two accounts concern different anchors of ReferentialContinuity. On the knowledge account, referential overlap and semantic similarity between adjacent sentences spare the reader a bridging inference, whereas the cue-utilisation account relies on connectives. In adults, semantic and causal relatedness dissociate by reader skill, with semantic relatedness weighing more for the less skilled reader [@todaroImpactSemanticCausal2010]. They also bear differently on processing time and on what is remembered [@wolfeCausalSemanticRelatedness2005]. The anchors need not therefore show the same age interaction, and a component interaction inside the region could arise from anchor interactions of opposite sign. Where the component posterior lies inside the region while the anchor interactions registered under Sensitivity analyses lie outside it with opposite signs, the equivalence verdict is retained and reported with that pattern. The sign of a coherence effect also depends on the cohesive device involved, so connectives enter the component by relation type, and the causal and contrastive densities are its connective anchors. The facilitation a connective affords was smaller for result relations than for concessive ones and differed between an analytic and a synthetic language [@marchalFacilitatingEffectConnectives2025], which supports both halves of that decision.

A negative interaction has a second interpretation under the Landscape model, which makes a reader's attempt at a bridging inference depend on the standard of coherence they bring to the text [@vandenbroekCognitiveProcessesDiscourse2017; @vandenbroekIntegratingMemorybasedConstructionist2005]. A reader who does not attempt it pays no time for the gap, so continuity would save the younger reader nothing if that band read to a lower standard. The online evidence limits that concern, since children of 8 to 13 made the local inferences a coherent representation required, if not the optional ones [@josephOnlineInferenceMaking2021]. This design does not separate a lower standard of coherence from cue utilisation, so @tbl-design treats a negative verdict as consistent with both.

As with Hypothesis 2, the existing evidence does not decide between the accounts. Eight- and ten-year-olds gained the same speed-up from an appropriate connective in self-paced reading, with the age interaction explicitly null across 91 children [@cainInfluenceConnectivesYoung2011]. No difference in online sensitivity to a coherence break was found between children of 8 to 9 and of 10 to 11 [@helderCoherenceMonitoringGood2016]. Among 8- to 10-year-olds reading two-clause sentences, the absence of the Dutch causal connective lengthened processing only for second-language readers with weaker syntactic knowledge [@vandenboschOnlineProcessingCausal2018]. The connective was worth most to the reader with the fewest resources, but the contrast between language backgrounds leaves age untested. In fourth graders, the effect of cohesion turned on world knowledge and far less on decoding skill, with age untestable within a single grade [@mcnamaraComprehensionChallengesFourth2011]. Where the studies we found at these ages manipulated whole-text coherence, they measured comprehension or inference, so none bears directly on reading rate. The three outcomes are interpreted as for Hypothesis 2.

The bottleneck-release account links the two age-band interactions. The smaller base that raises the proportional grammatical cost in the older band also enlarges the proportional continuity saving there. The account predicts a positive Hypothesis 2 interaction, a negative Hypothesis 3 interaction and a negative or null LexicalDifficulty × AgeBand interaction. Differential attrition and a larger non-reading share in the younger band, both described above, would produce the same signs for Hypotheses 2 and 3. Each, however, would push the lexical interaction positive, the one sign that bottleneck release excludes. We will report the joint pattern of these three tier-1 estimates descriptively, and no verdict depends on it.

Both registered age-band interactions are averaged over languages whose writing systems differ in type and in depth, and the age band does not mean the same thing in each. In most European orthographies, children read familiar words accurately and fluently within the first school year, whereas development is more than twice as slow in English and lags in French and Portuguese [@seymourFoundationLiteracyAcquisition2003]. Psycholinguistic grain size theory derives that pattern from how consistently a writing system represents phonology, which sets the size of the units a learner comes to rely on [@zieglerReadingAcquisitionDevelopmental2005]. Children matched on years of instruction show orthography-specific length and frequency signatures, with English qualitatively unlike German and Finnish, while adults converge [@schroederEyeMovementsChildren2022]. Between two transparent orthographies, the developmental trajectory can nonetheless be comparable, with language-specific effects confined to morphological complexity [@marziComparableReadingDevelopment2026], so the heterogeneity expected here is a matter of degree. Children reading different orthographies are therefore at different points on the automatisation curve. On the bottleneck-release account, the developmental signature would be largest where decoding automatises latest. The registered coefficient is a prevalence-weighted average across those positions, and we do not generalise it from any one orthography [@shareAnglocentricitiesCurrentReading2008].

*Hypothesis 4: narration and selective attenuation.* We predict that the LexicalDifficulty coefficient will be proportionally smaller under narration than the ReferentialContinuity coefficient is. With $\pi_{\text{lex}}$ and $\pi_{\text{cont}}$ denoting each coefficient's proportional attenuation under narration, computed draw by draw as set out under Confirmatory models, the prediction is that $\pi_{\text{lex}} - \pi_{\text{cont}} > 0.20$. The threshold is four times the region's half-width and is a registered convention. The prediction follows from the decoding-scaffolding account. A spoken rendition supplies word identity without print-to-sound mapping, the step that a low-frequency or long word makes expensive. The rendition does not supply the link between two ideas, which the reader must still construct. The benefit of text-to-speech is largest for children whose decoding is weak but whose language is intact [@keelorImpactTexttospeechFeatures2023]. In 34 children aged 8 to 9, the time saved by the audio fell on the first encounter with an orthographically novel word and had gone by the second [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024]. Besides word identity, a voice conveys prosodic phrasing, which a silent reader must project [@breenEmpiricalInvestigationsImplicit2014] and which is still developing across the primary years [@goddeReviewReadingProsody2020]. Narration could thereby lower the grammatical coefficient by a route unrelated to word identity. Prosodic phrasing does not, however, supply the link between two sentences, so the contrast between the lexical and continuity attenuations remains interpretable. The grammatical-by-narration interaction is reported for description only.

Whether narration spares the reader the decoding cost depends on timing. In reading while listening, adults' eyes generally ran ahead of the audio and rarely rested on the word being heard [@conklinWhatEyetrackingTells2020]. Among 119 learners of English, the multimodal condition ran slightly slower than reading alone [@maloneEyeMovementsItem2025], whereas children of 8 to 9 showed the opposite pattern [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024]. The decoding account describes a reader slower than the audio, and the competing audio-pacing account a reader faster than it. The full-sample contrast shows which kind of reader predominates in the narrated sessions.

On the pacing account, the audio's duration sets narrated reading time, so each narrated slope converges on the slope of audio duration per word. That slope is near zero for referential continuity and positive for lexical properties tied to word length, since a word with more syllables takes longer to speak. The two attenuations are therefore equal only once that duration is accounted for, and otherwise the pacing account predicts $\pi_{\text{lex}} - \pi_{\text{cont}}$ at or below zero. Reading aloud runs at about 183 words per minute, against 238 to 260 for silent reading, and the gap between text types is predicted by word length [@brysbaertHowManyWords2019]. Pacing alone fails to flatten word-level effects, since manipulating reading speed left the influence of word properties on eye movements in place [@schwalmTestingSpeedaccuracyTradeoff2026]. That result partly motivates the registered contrast between the lexical and continuity attenuations.

The compression diagnostic withholds the full-sample verdict where the audio sets the pace for most narrated sessions. An adjustment for the audio's duration allows for the mixture that the diagnostic can miss, in which only some narrated sessions are paced. The adjustment rests on a predicted spoken duration per word, defined under Materials and computed from the texts before any outcome is linked to them. The refit including it is registered under Sensitivity analyses.

The pacing account has substantial support. The meta-analytic comprehension benefit reported above is confined to comparisons with experimenter-paced reading [@clintonlisellDoesReadingWhile2023]. A registered report testing the resource-freeing mechanism in 86 adult second-language readers found comprehension *worse* under narration than in silent reading [@huiForcedPaceReading2026]. In the same study, individual differences in orthographic decoding and speech segmentation did not interact with input condition in the way that mechanism predicts. In 21 secondary-school students with dyslexia and 22 without, audio support increased reading time in most tasks while leaving comprehension unchanged [@knoopvancampenEffectAudiosupportStrategy2021]. Where measured incidentally, the compression is severe, with the standard deviation of exposure time falling from 11.56 seconds when self-paced to 0.62 seconds when narrated [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024]. The tests we found concern comprehension and the variance of exposure time, and none bears on the contrast that Hypothesis 4 registers.

A third possibility, with the same predictions as the pacing account, is that the child listens without reading, so that the interval is the audio's duration plus the page turns. Attention to print is low in preschoolers listening to a storybook [@evansWhatChildrenAre2005] and rises across the primary grades with reading skill [@roycharlandEyeMovementsShared2007]. In older children reading an illustrated story in a second language, audio moved the eyes from the text to the pictures without changing comprehension [@pellicersanchezYoungLearnersProcessing2020; @serranoYoungL2Learners2022]. By contrast, 8- to 9-year-olds did fixate the words under bimodal presentation [@valentiniReadingWhileListening2024]. The share of narrated sessions in which the child read along is unknown and likely to differ by age band. The logs cannot separate a paced reading from a listening. An inside-region verdict is therefore reported as time set by the audio, whether or not the child read along, and never as evidence that the narrated sessions involved reading. Listening without reading is ruled out by definition only in the narrated sessions that the audio cannot have paced, the unpaced subset defined under Confirmatory models.

The flag records the voice setting at the end of a session (question (a) in @tbl-unresolved). A narrated session is therefore one in which narration was available, not necessarily one in which the child listened, and a setting changed during the session is recorded only in its final state. Under the rule registered for that answer, the Hypothesis 4 contrast is an intention-to-treat comparison. Sessions misclassified in this way, and children who ignored the audio, dilute both attenuations towards zero, and the dilution is stated wherever the coefficient is reported.

The Hypothesis 4 contrast is also exposed to selection into narration state. With narration on in about nine sessions in ten, the unnarrated slopes, the denominators of both attenuation proportions, are estimated largely from the families who chose to switch the audio off. If the children reading without audio are disproportionately the fluent readers, their slopes are attenuated by selection and both proportions are distorted. The data contain no measure of reading skill with which to adjust for this, so we will report narration prevalence by age band, reading level and language before fitting. The rule under Confirmatory models makes the within-account contrast the primary estimate where the data allow. Because both proportions are ratios, the contrast is evaluated only under the Hypothesis 4 precondition, that fewer than 5 per cent of the draws of each unnarrated slope, lexical and continuity, lie inside the region. If either slope fails the precondition, there is no attenuation to compare and Hypothesis 4 is reported as not evaluable. The precondition does not depend on the sign of any coefficient.

The four outcomes, their posterior criteria and their interpretations are registered in @tbl-design and under Decision rules.

*Hypothesis 5: text properties and the difficulty rating.* We predict that, in an ordinal model of the post-reading rating, LexicalDifficulty and GrammaticalLoad will be associated with higher odds of a harder rating and ReferentialContinuity with lower odds, each by an odds ratio outside the region. We further predict that the three standardised coefficients will rank by magnitude as they do in the reading-time model. Two measures of the same three constructs, one behavioural and one judgement-based, obtained on different scales from overlapping sets of children, need not rank those constructs the same way. Their agreement on order is therefore a substantive prediction of the theory object, on which both measures record the same expended effort.

The link between the two measures rests on the effort heuristic of Koriat's cue-utilisation approach to metacognitive judgement. On that approach, a judgement of difficulty is inferred from cues such as experienced effort and does not directly reflect processing [@koriatMonitoringOnesOwn1997; @undorfJudgmentsLearningReflect2011]. Two meta-analyses put the association between experienced effort and monitoring judgements at *r* = -.36 and, in a meta-analytic structural model, at $\beta$ = -.19 [@baarsRelationStudentsEffort2020; @davidRelationPerceivedMental2024]. Those are judgements of learning and of confidence, so for a difficulty rating the sign is reversed. Second, third and fifth graders were less confident in an answer the longer they had taken to choose it, and reliance on that cue was stronger in the older children [@koriatChoiceLatencyCue2010]. The rating would then be a later report of the same expended effort that reading time measures, not a separate measurement of the text. Effort is attributed to the material when the material imposes it, but not when a learner chooses to invest it, a distinction established in adult learners [@koriatIntricateRelationshipsMonitoring2006; @koriatJudgmentsLearningDepend2014]. In children, consistent with that distinction, the association between effort and judgement weakens where regulation is goal driven [@baarsRelationStudentsEffort2020].

Partly because reading in this app is self-paced and voluntary, the rating is registered here as a measure under test. On the same grounds, the theory object marks this prediction as diagnostic against the engagement account. Convergence in the predicted directions weighs against that account. Its absence is interpreted, under the rule in @tbl-design, as a failure of the rating and not as support for the engagement account.

That approach also suggests why the two measures might diverge. A judgement made after finishing draws on the cues still accessible at that moment, and the three sources of demand are not equally accessible. Word-level difficulty recurs at every line, whereas the cost of an unstated link between ideas is spread over the text. Consistent with this, a cohesion manipulation that moved paragraph-level judgements left whole-text judgements untouched unless readers could still consult the text [@lefevreTextCohesionMetacomprehension2004]. In adults predicting their own recall, however, judgements about a whole text did rise with coherence [@rawsonArePerformancePredictions2002]. The posterior probability that the two measures rank the components alike is the study's principal convergent-validity check, evaluated against the 0.90 criterion under Decision rules.

The evidence closest to this rating concerns related judgements, mostly those children make about their own learning and comprehension. Among children of 8 to 10 solving arithmetic problems, the mental effort they reported investing was related to their judgements of learning, which tracked the complexity of the problem [@baarsAccuracyPrimarySchool2018]. Children in both of this study's age bands judge how well they have understood a text [@steinerDevelopmentChildrensMonitoring2020], and fifth graders do so both for the whole text and for individual answers [@markovichMetacognitiveMonitoringReading2026]. Primary-school children are more overconfident in those judgements than secondary-school children [@mirandolaMetacognitiveMonitoringText2018], but that overconfidence depends on the text. Among 407 primary and secondary students, the primary children overestimated their performance on expository passages and inferential questions but calibrated as well as the older students on narrative texts [@zagatoHowSureAm2026]. Every text in this study is narrative. Comprehension judgements concern the reader's own understanding, whereas the rating here asks about the text. In adults, subjective comprehensibility ratings of narrative text can be predicted from computed text features [@tilmatinePredictingSubjectiveRatings2024]. None of the child metacognition literature we found validates a global post-reading judgement of a text's difficulty against the text's measured properties in children of this age. We likewise found no psychometric evaluation of the three-point format, a classroom heuristic whose options are easy, just right and difficult.

Children's monitoring judgements are internally consistent when aggregated over items, their reliability is limited by that of the first-order task, and their accuracy varies from one task to another [@roebersExploringPsychometricProperties2021; @eberhartMetacognitiveMonitoringEarly2025]. The design therefore aggregates ratings at text level and applies the five-rater floor registered under Confirmatory models. Children of 6 to 13 have a limited grasp of multi-point response formats, and word-anchored options agree better with a yes-or-no standard than numeric ones do [@mellorUseLikertScales2014]. The number of options bears on how reliably children and young adolescents answer, with four options proving optimal and seven or more lowering reliability [@borgersResponseEffectsSurveys2004]. Which way any of this would move a three-point rating inside an app is not established, so we register the direction as unknown and report the observed distribution. Equating reported difficulty with expended effort is contestable. In 80 children aged 8 to 12, the difficulty and effort ratings given after a battery of cognitive tasks were uncorrelated with each other and only weakly related to performance [@torresMetacognitiveRatingsCognitive2026].

With age, children come to judge a task by the effort it cost. In self-paced learning, judgements of learning fell as study time rose for third, fifth and sixth graders (mean ages 8.9 to 12.0) but not for first and second graders (mean ages 7.0 and 7.9) [@koriatMemorizingEffortHeuristic2009]. The authors place that division at about 8.5 years, near this study's age-band boundary, but their finding does not show whether direct judgements of a text divide the same way. A rating that tracks the text at 7 to 8 remains possible, because even 5- and 6-year-olds use an item's difficulty adaptively when evaluating their own performance [@vanloonDevelopmentalProgressionPerformance2017]. The rating model includes the same component-by-age-band terms as the reading-time model, but its registered tests remain the pooled odds ratios and the ordering. The band-specific odds ratios derived from those terms are descriptive, as stated under Confirmatory models. Recorded age bands in the structural sample skewed towards the younger band (Supplementary Section S8), so a prevalence-weighted pooled odds ratio will be weighted towards that band. @tbl-design accordingly interprets a pooled odds ratio inside the region, together with an older-band odds ratio outside it, as a limit on the rating specific to the younger band.

The effective sample size is the number of distinct children rating each text, which the raw count of ratings overstates, so the model has a varying intercept for Text. We will report the intraclass correlation for the rating at text level as a reliability estimate for this format. Before fitting, we will report the distribution of raters per text and the distribution of the three rating categories overall and by age band and language. The category distribution will be reported again alongside any inside-region verdict, because a distribution concentrated in one category limits what a cumulative logit can resolve.

A failure here is ambiguous on its own, since it could lie in the rating or in the components. Because Hypothesis 1 resolves the ambiguity, the interpretations in @tbl-design are conditioned on the reading-time coefficients. Components that predict reading time but not the rating leave the feature pipeline sound. Partial convergence in @tbl-design, with directions as predicted but an ordering probability below 0.90, does not call the components into question. The design analysis marks this hypothesis as the one most likely to be underpowered. If it is declared underpowered, or its verdict is inconclusive, the ordering is reported descriptively and convergent validity is recorded as not established. This rule gives the fifth outcome-neutral check a defined outcome whether or not Hypothesis 5 reaches a verdict. An inconclusive verdict from the census of existing records is still informative, because it sets an upper limit on the reliability a single-item difficulty rating can have at the availability such apps achieve.

*Hypothesis 6: accumulated reading and reading pace.* We predict that, among children with several recorded sessions, a one-standard-deviation within-child increase in accumulated in-app reading, on its log scale, will be associated with a reduction in log reading time per word. The reduction is predicted over and above session order, the interval since the previous session and the time since the child's first session. Measures defines the within-child standard deviation, the unit for which the region under Decision rules is stated. For each language, we will report the change implied by a doubling of one plus the accumulated stories. It equals the coefficient multiplied by $\ln 2$ and divided by that language's within-child standard deviation of accumulated reading.

On the orthographic-learning account, each successful encounter with a written word form is an opportunity to acquire or sharpen the word-specific orthographic representation supporting its later recognition [@sharePhonologicalRecodingSelfteaching1995]. Under the Lexical Quality Hypothesis, the quality of those representations makes skilled word reading cheap [@perfettiReadingAbilityLexical2007]. Print experience is accordingly treated as the main source of growth in word reading [@nationNurturingLexicalLegacy2017; @castlesEndingReadingWars2018; @deaconTestingMechanismsUnderlying2024]. Because the mechanism operates on items, exposure is counted in words of completed distinct stories, and repeated readings are reserved for the practice analysis under Sensitivity analyses. Each further form adds less as the lexicon fills, so accumulated reading enters on a log scale.

Learning of this kind is primarily item-based. In grades 1 and 2, at or just below the younger band, children who met novel spellings in short stories learned them, but transferred that learning clearly only to orthographically related forms [@tuckerEarlySelfteaching2025]. Across 62 experiments, the outcome of such learning is modulated by language-specific word properties [@liSystematicReviewOrthographic2023]. Reading one story can make the next cheaper by two routes, the words the two texts share and the sublexical regularities a reader generalises from them [@castlesEndingReadingWars2018]. The size of the association is therefore limited by how much of a new text earlier reading can already have made easier. Both limits are looser for stories written to one reading level than for texts sampled at large, and neither is measured here.

Outside English, orthographic learning, lexical knowledge, reading fluency and spelling were associated in German-speaking primary-school children [@schmalzDoFasterLearners2025]. The account's implications differ between languages, because decoding automatises at very different ages across European orthographies [@seymourFoundationLiteracyAcquisition2003], as the paragraph on orthographic depth above records. On a model in which decipherability precedes unitisation and automatisation [@shareBlueprintUniversalTheory2025], the per-unit speed-up that accumulated reading affords should be shallower where decoding was automatised earlier. The pooled deviation coefficient remains the registered test. The per-language slopes from the secondary refit under Sensitivity analyses will be reported descriptively alongside it, annotated with orthographic depth. @seymourFoundationLiteracyAcquisition2003 place eight of the app's languages on five ordered levels of depth but omit the other eleven. Polish will be annotated at the middle level, beside Dutch and Portuguese [@awramiukReadingSpellingAcquisition2013; @schuppertWriteYouSpeak2017], and Korean as shallow in the reading direction [@leeRelationsMorphologicalAwareness2023; @leachmanRelationTextReading2025]. Indonesian, Romanian and Turkish will be annotated as shallow, and Russian, like Korean, as shallow in the reading direction [@borleffsMeasuringOrthographicTransparency2017; @doleanLanguageSkillsNot2021; @siegelmanExpandingHorizonsCrosslinguistic2022; @rakhlinPhonemicAwarenessIs2014]. Arabic, Hebrew, Thai and Chinese are annotated by type of writing system, since a scale built to order European alphabets does not order them. Supplementary Section S3 gives the evidence for every placement, all of them fixed with the feature inventory.

As noted earlier, practice and skill are reciprocal over years [@torppaLeisureReadingNot2020; @vanbergenHowArePractice2021], so the coefficient estimates a within-window association, not a practice effect. Random-intercept cross-lagged models on more than 5,100 German secondary students found no within-person evidence that reading more yields better reading competence, while the reverse path, from competence to exposure, remained [@bittmannReadingBegetsReading2025]. Only a design that separates within-person change from stable between-person differences can show such an asymmetry. The within-child deviation and the account-mean term separate them by definition. For the path from reading to skill, exposure to a text experimentally speeded skilled adults' later recognition of the low-frequency words in it [@chetailReadingBooksPositive2024]. That study, the closest experimental demonstration we found, is confined to adults and to rare words. Reciprocity established at yearly lags does not by itself license treating the reverse path as negligible over a window of months.

Within the window, a child whose session went slowly may not return, so later sessions would over-represent children whose earlier sessions went well, which would push the coefficient in the predicted direction. The family of a child reading faster may choose longer stories or raise the reading level. Either change alters the composition of what accumulates, even though the current story's length and level are adjusted for. Before the coefficient is interpreted, we will report the distribution of each user account's final-session pace relative to that account's own mean, and the number of accounts whose reading level changed within the window. The audit under Sampling plan establishes that number in any case. Two refits will be reported with the registered term, and no verdict depends on either. One will exclude every account's final eligible session, and the other will add the previous session's standardised pace as a covariate, by analogy with the random-intercept cross-lagged model [@hamakerCritiqueCrosslaggedPanel2015]. Because conditioning on a lagged outcome alongside an Account intercept is biased in short series, the lagged-pace refit constrains the size of the concern without resolving it.

The account-mean term is reported, but it tests neither the orthographic-learning account nor its reverse-path rival. Both predict it negative, since a child who has read more in the app may read faster for having done so and a child who reads faster may go on reading. How much and how well children read have long been associated at the between-person level [@molReadNotRead2011]. Only the within-child deviation separates the two accounts, and the rival is substantive. In three twin samples, the modelled direction of causation ran from reading ability, literacy skill or comprehension to print exposure or literacy enjoyment, with the reverse influence zero in one sample [@vanbergenWhyChildrenRead2018; @vanbergenLiteracySkillsSeem2023; @erbeliUnravelingRelationReading2020].

Each covariate addresses a named alternative. Session order absorbs familiarity with the interface and with the generator's story schemas, since a reader who knows the shape of a story reads it faster for reasons the orthographic-learning account does not claim. Days since the previous session absorbs spacing, and days since the first session absorbs maturation and schooling. Once the three are held constant, with session order entered as its logarithm under Measures, the accumulated-reading deviation is identified by within-child variation in the lengths of the stories already read. That variation is small where the reading level fixes story length. Partly for that reason, Design and precision analysis re-derives the tier-2 requirement before fitting, at the observed distribution of sessions per child and with the three covariates added. Oral reading fluency grows appreciably and unevenly over a school year [@christCurriculumbasedMeasurementOral2010], so an elapsed-time covariate absorbs maturation only if growth is close to linear in days within a child and the window's position in the school year is immaterial. Growth rates differ between children, and the variables that predict those rates [@khanolainenPredictingReadingFluency2024] predict how much a child reads as well. Before Hypothesis 6 is interpreted, we will report the within-child correlation matrix of the three covariates and the deviation term, with their variance inflation factors. At the same stage, we will report the calendar month of each session as a descriptive stratifier, to identify any window spanning a school holiday. @tbl-design gives the interpretation of each outcome for the deviation term.

Every hypothesis is labelled by the rules under Decision rules, and an inconclusive result is reported as such. No hypothesis is filtered by a preliminary significance test, but three labels take precedence over a verdict. A hypothesis is declared untestable if its component fails the construction rule under Outcome-blind dimension reduction or if its outcome or contrast is absent from the frozen extract. Hypothesis 6 is also declared untestable if account identifiers in the transferred extract remain in floating-point notation, as set out under Data provenance. That label is assigned before the model is fitted and without reference to any coefficient. A hypothesis whose data fall below its precision threshold in @tbl-design, as re-derived where Design and precision analysis says so, is instead declared underpowered. Its model is still fitted and reported, and no conclusion is drawn from an interval the design analysis predicted would be indeterminate. A hypothesis is reported as not evaluable when a registered post-fitting contingency removes its test. Only two contingencies do so: failure of the Hypothesis 4 precondition and failure of the positive control on recorded reading time. Where the data controller's answers to the questions in @tbl-unresolved falsify an auxiliary assumption, the affected predictions are reassigned by the rules in that table, never reinterpreted after the fact.

Whatever the verdicts, this study will not identify a causal effect of any text property, age band or narration setting. Nor will it estimate how fast children in general read, or generalise beyond families who chose to install and use this application. Its confirmatory results will say nothing about comprehension, since none of the contingent hypotheses is activated at submission. The constraints on generality are these: children aged 7 and over who read narrative texts of a few hundred words on a touchscreen, in one of the app's 19 languages, inside one commercial application [@simonsConstraintsGeneralityCOG2017]. One generator wrote the generated stories in English, and machine translation rendered them in every other language. Outside English, the generated texts are therefore machine-translated prose, and the associations estimated there are associations with such texts.

The medium is one of those constraints, and it is not neutral. Reading on screen yields poorer comprehension than reading the same text on paper, with the shortfall larger under time pressure and for informational text [@delgadoDontThrowAway2018]. In children, the paper advantage holds except where a digital text adds features aligned with the content [@furenesComparisonChildrensReading2021]. A network meta-analysis of 56 samples locates most of that shortfall in scrolling [@clintonlisellDecodingDigitalReading2026]. Where scrolling was required, paper outperformed every device by 0.35 to 0.48 standard deviations. Where it was not, the differences ran from 0.03 to 0.12 and were unreliable, and a tablet read without scrolling ranked closest to paper [@clintonlisellDecodingDigitalReading2026]. This app presents a story as pages on a tablet, so the largest known moderator of the screen shortfall does not apply here. The laboratory results underlying the three components were obtained largely on paper, so the comparison drawn here spans a change of medium as well as of setting. A coefficient smaller than its laboratory counterpart may reflect either change.

# Methods

## Ethics information

This research complies with all relevant ethical regulations. The data are generated in the ordinary operation of a commercial application and collected by its publisher under the terms of use and privacy policy a family accepts on installation. A parent or guardian registers consent in the app for research use of anonymised records. That registration is the informed consent under which the records are transferred to us, and no further consent is sought. We play no part in collection, have no contact with any child or family and return nothing to the platform, so nothing done here can alter what any child experiences. No compensation is provided or applicable.

The extract contains no direct identifier. It records no name, contact detail, precise location or device identifier, and accounts appear in it only as pseudonymous strings generated by the platform. Ethical approval for secondary analysis of these anonymised records [has been granted by / is being sought from] the Departmental Research Ethics Committee of the Department of Education, University of Oxford (reference [to be inserted]). Approval will be in place before in-principle acceptance. The study involves no experimental manipulation or intervention, so no question of withdrawal from a procedure arises. A family's right to have its records erased is exercised through the platform. Any erasure between building the extract and transferring it will be recorded by the data controller and reported at Stage 2.

## Pilot data

The pilot material comprises the data dictionary, a 35-row structural sample of the session table and a summary of that sample computed with the count script described under Data provenance. We received the sample and the dictionary from the data controller on 27 July 2026 to confirm the shape of the table, and computed the summary on 6 August 2026. The sample contains real reading times for 35 sessions on five distinct texts, one session per account, in ten of the app's 19 reading languages. It cannot be used to test any hypothesis, since none is identified by 35 observations and no within-child term is estimable from one session per account. The sample nevertheless fixed two inputs to the design analysis, the rating availability (present in 10 of 35) and the narration prevalence (on in 32 of 35), whose imbalance roughly triples the Hypothesis 4 requirement. The age band was blank in 10 sessions, a gap that question (h) in @tbl-unresolved takes up. Supplementary Section S8 reports the sample and its summary in full, and the sample is deposited for peer review as the Data availability statement describes.

## Design

### Data provenance, sequestration and outcome blindness

The data this protocol analyses already exist. Nature Human Behaviour considers secondary analyses of existing data on condition that authors can evidence no prior access to the data in question. We put the arrangement set out below to the journal's editorial office, which confirmed it as appropriate on 3 August 2026.

The data controller builds the extract on its own schedule and holds it. No part of the extract will be transferred to us until the journal confirms in-principle acceptance in writing. Until then, and with the editorial office's agreement, three items may be sent to us: a manifest, the story texts and the provider-computed counts. The manifest is the record that the count script described below keeps of each file it reads: the file's name, size, column list, row count, range of session dates and SHA-256 checksum. With it, the file eventually transferred can be shown to be the one that was built. The certification in Supplementary Section S7 states the build date and the window the extract covers. The story texts are identified by story identifier, reading language, reading level and app version, and their page breaks are preserved. They may be received before in-principle acceptance because every linguistic measure is computed on them and none contains a behavioural outcome.

The provider-computed counts are aggregates that the data controller obtains from the extract by running a count script we supplied. The count script reads nineteen columns besides reading time, writes one small table of counts and a readable web page drawn from it, and never reports a reading time as a value. Both the version sent on 7 August 2026 and a revised version, sent on 18 September 2026, are deposited with this protocol. The revision adds checks against malformed input, among them a count of identifiers in floating-point notation, and extends the first version's record of each file read. On the structural sample and on clean synthetic exports, it reproduces every count of the first version. The two differ where the first version misread an input, for example by filing a session under its story title when the story identifier was empty. The data controller has been asked to run the revised version, because two rules below use its check of the account identifiers.

A count computed from an outcome column could compromise blindness, so the script treats reading time only as a column whose usability has to be established. It reports how many values are absent, non-numeric, negative or zero, how many fall into each of seven bands bounded by successive powers of ten, and how many distinct values the column contains. The script also reports the largest number of sessions sharing any single value, and it never crosses reading time with language, age, text, account or date. Supplementary Table 6 shows its output on the structural sample. Bands this coarse cannot distinguish a fast text from a slow one, but they do distinguish a column recorded in seconds from one recorded in milliseconds. The analysis cannot be specified until the column's unit is known. A session-timeout cap would appear as a large number of sessions sharing one value, and the censoring rule under Sampling plan depends on that count.

In the structural sample, account identifiers were written in floating-point notation with six significant digits (Supplementary Section S8), a form in which distinct accounts can share a value. The revised script therefore counts the sessions whose account or story identifier is still in that notation. If any account identifier is in that notation, the script marks the account figures as unreliable and asks for the identifiers to be re-exported as integers or as text. If identifiers in that notation remain in the transferred extract, accounts cannot be told apart reliably, and neither tier 2 nor the within-account narration contrast can be formed. Hypothesis 6 is then declared untestable, and no other analysis of tier 2 is run. Tier 1 is still analysed, without the Account intercept, as when the Account rule under Sampling plan is not met. The restriction to first readings and the five-rater floor are applied to the identifiers as recorded.

At submission, we hold the English story texts, received on 1 October 2026. The texts in the other languages, and the manifest and the provider-computed counts, [had been received on DATE / had not yet been received]. The number of distinct texts with eligible readings cannot be established before the audit of the frozen extract, so @tbl-unresolved reports it as unresolved and sets out how it will be established.

Two conventions apply throughout this protocol. First, five inputs decide whether a hypothesis is tested, on which sample and with which model. They are the provider-computed counts, the audit of the frozen extract, the output of the prior-derivation pipeline, the data controller's written answers and the thresholds registered here. No fitted quantity enters these decisions except through the post-fitting rules listed under Decision rules. Second, wherever the text says a quantity will be reported, it will be reported in the Stage 2 manuscript whether or not it changes a conclusion.

A descriptive study of an earlier 30-day window on this platform, published by two of the authors, used only summaries the data controller prepared [@ratnerProductiveStruggleChildrens2026]. That study, described in the Introduction, relates no text property to any behaviour, analyses no reading duration and informs no decision registered here. The structural sample and its summary are disclosed under Pilot data.

At the editorial office's direction, we have not run the dimension reduction specified below and will not run it before submission, although we hold the story texts from which its inputs are computed. The component solution is fully specified but unfitted.

The data controller will supply a signed copy of the certification reproduced in Supplementary Section S7. The document states the held extract's build date, window, row count and checksums and names its owner and a deputy. It certifies that no part of the extract has been or will be transferred to the research team, or to anyone acting for it, before written confirmation of in-principle acceptance. A final clause states that no analysis relating story text to reading time has been conducted by the data controller or reported to the team.

### Materials

The reading materials are the story texts, each written by a generative model around the combination of five attributes a family chooses. Families may also choose a story from a classic set. For each reading, the extract records whether the text was generated or classic, the reading level served, the language, the app version and the page count. Every session will be linked to the features of the exact version it was served, matched on story identifier, reading language, reading level and app version.

Every text coefficient is identified by comparing texts, so how much this design can establish depends on the number of distinct texts with eligible readings, which is not yet known. The data controller's estimate spans a few hundred to a few million, depending on whether a combination of attributes yields one shared text or a new text for each session. The evidence favours shared texts. The platform's published description reports a catalogue of over 40,000 generated English-language stories, many of them translated into the child's home language [@ratnerDidRobotWrite2025]. In the structural sample, the story identifiers of two attribute combinations recurred across 11 and 7 of the 35 accounts (Supplementary Section S8). A recurring identifier cannot show whether the text behind it was regenerated, however, so we put question (d) in @tbl-unresolved to the data controller. Its answer, received in October 2026, is that each story is generated once in English, translated into the other languages by machine translation and stored, and that every reader of a given version sees the same text. Under the rule the table registers for that answer, the models include a varying intercept for the underlying story, crossed with Language.

For every text, we will compute features in four families. *Lexical* features are mean log frequency of content words, the proportion of words with a frequency below one per million tokens on the uniform frequency resource, mean rated age of acquisition and mean orthographic length. Mean per-word surprisal under a language-specific neural language model, lexical density, lexical diversity and concreteness complete the family. Diversity is the moving-average type-token ratio over a 50-token window, and its per-language correlation with the Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity will be reported. A word's surprisal is the sum of the surprisals of the subword tokens composing it, and the mean is taken over the same whitespace-delimited words as the outcome's denominator. *Grammatical* features are mean dependency distance from a universal-dependencies parse, clauses per sentence, the ratio of subordinate to main clauses, mean sentence length and mean depth of noun-phrase modification. *Discourse* features are mean semantic similarity between adjacent sentences from a multilingual sentence encoder, referential overlap, connectives per hundred words by relation type and narrativity. Referential overlap is the proportion of adjacent sentence pairs sharing at least one content lemma in a nominal position, which operationalises the argument-overlap rule of the construction-integration model without a coreference resolver. Narrativity is a stipulated composite of past-tense marking, personal pronouns and direct speech, defined in Supplementary Table 3. *Affective* features are the mean and the variability of valence and of arousal. One further text quantity serves Hypothesis 4 alone, a predicted spoken duration per word on a log scale, computed from syllables per word plus sentence- and clause-boundary pauses per word from punctuation. Its resources and matched-token proportion are given in Supplementary Table 3. If the data controller supplies the audio's duration for every eligible text, the logarithm of that duration per word replaces the prediction, because the pacing account concerns the audio's actual duration. The prediction is then kept for a sensitivity analysis. Durations supplied for only some texts serve a sensitivity analysis restricted to them.

The extract records narration only as a session-level flag. The data controller confirmed in October 2026 that the flag holds the voice setting at the end of the session, so it shows that narration was available, not that it played. The platform has not disclosed how the audio is produced or presented. Two undisclosed properties bear on the interpretation of a narrated session. Word-level highlighting couples the eye to the voice, although the evidence comes from children younger than any here [@liaoElectronicStorybookDesign2020]. A page that advances when playback ends would make a narrated session's duration largely the audio's duration. Question (a) in @tbl-unresolved lists these and the remaining items with the consequence of each answer. Any item established from the public version of the app is reported as observed, with the date. Observing the app involves no outcome data, and none of these facts enters a model.

Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 give the primary and the sensitivity resource for each feature family, with their coverage across the app's 19 languages. Four rules govern the tables and are fixed before any feature is computed. First, each feature will be computed from a single resource applied identically in every language, even where a better native resource exists in one of them. Native norms will be run as a pre-specified sensitivity analysis, and their correlation with the single-resource values will be reported for each language. Second, no value is transferred across languages by translating a word list. A predicted resource is admitted only where the prediction was made within each language by one documented procedure and its correlation with native ratings is reported. Where no acceptable measure exists for a language, that language does not contribute that feature.

Third, every measure reports the proportion of tokens it matched, and a language in which a measure matches fewer than 80 per cent of content-word tokens does not contribute it. Content-word tokens are those whose universal part-of-speech tag is NOUN, VERB, ADJ or ADV. The token-coverage rule differs from the text-coverage rule under Outcome-blind dimension reduction, and the two can reach opposite decisions on the same feature. Where some languages lack a feature, that family's pooled solution is computed on the features common to every contributing language. Such a feature enters only the per-language descriptive solutions and the language-specific sensitivity analyses. The first rule has two exceptions, concreteness and age of acquisition. No uniform concreteness resource meets the second rule, and the one cross-linguistic age-of-acquisition set has only 299 words, too few to yield a text mean. Both are therefore taken from native norms where these meet the third rule, and Outcome-blind dimension reduction sets out how they enter the component solutions.

Fourth, the full inventory, the software versions, the model checkpoints, the tokenisation rules and the matched-token proportions will be frozen and published before any feature is linked to outcome data. Sentence segmentation is registered with them: pages are concatenated with a single space, and a page break is never a sentence boundary. Supplementary Section S3 lists the per-language segmentation diagnostics to be reported. The four rules constrain Korean most, and the same section sets out the consequences for it after Supplementary Table 3.

Proper nouns are excluded from the content-word denominator of the third rule and from every norm-based mean, because the platform puts invented names into every story. The hero, the companion and the setting a family chose are named in the text, and no subtitle frequency list, age-of-acquisition norm or concreteness norm contains an invented name. Those names recur through the story, so we will report three length-normalised name quantities from the same universal-dependencies parse. They are the proportion of tokens tagged as proper nouns, the number of distinct proper-noun types per hundred words and the mean repetitions per type. Each norm-based mean is reported with and without the exclusion, together with the two versions' correlation within each language. Surprisal is computed with the names present in context and excluded only from the mean.

### Measures

The processing outcome, serving Hypotheses 1 to 4 and 6, is the natural logarithm of elapsed reading time divided by the story's word count, standardised within reading language. Hypothesis 5 has a separate outcome, the child's optional post-reading rating of the story as easy, just right or difficult, treated as ordered and modelled on a cumulative-logit scale. A word, in the processing outcome's denominator and in every per-word quantity, is a whitespace-delimited token of the text as served. Chinese and Thai do not separate words with spaces, so in those languages a word is a token of the frozen word segmenter of the pipeline registered for the language in Supplementary Table 4. In most of the other languages, the token is an ordinary word. In Korean, it is an eojeol, a content word with its postpositional particles or verbal endings, which is the unit of the Korean dependency treebanks and of both parsers in Supplementary Table 3. A Korean text therefore contains fewer tokens than a translation of it would, so for the same content a Korean rate in words per minute is lower and not comparable with the other languages. The same holds to a lesser degree in Arabic and Hebrew, which write the article and some prepositions and conjunctions as prefixes, and in Turkish, whose words carry chains of suffixes. Of the plausibility bounds under Sampling plan, the fast one excludes fewer readings in these languages and the slow one more. Associations in each language are interpreted through its own language-varying slopes throughout.

The per-word scale also ties the outcome to word length. Mean orthographic length anchors LexicalDifficulty and helps determine how many words a text contains, since the same content in longer words needs fewer of them. As a result, time per word rises with word length even where time per character is unchanged. The per-character refit under Sensitivity analyses removes that dependence without altering the primary scale. Where the extract includes the platform's own word count, we will report its agreement with ours before any outcome model is fitted.

The outcome's intraclass correlations at the Text and the Account level will be reported from the tier-1 variance components. They give the reliability with which a text and an account are characterised by their readings.

The confirmatory predictors are the three component scores defined under Outcome-blind dimension reduction. Text length in words, narrativity, mean valence and mean arousal are pre-specified secondary text predictors and enter every model as covariates. Valence and arousal effects on word-recognition latency are larger among low-frequency words [@kupermanEmotionLanguageValence2014], so the affective means overlap LexicalDifficulty and enter only as adjustments. Omitted, they would leave part of that component's association unadjusted. No interaction between an affective mean and a component is estimated, and the variance inflation factors under Decision rules will show the overlap. Every affective value used here descends from adult ratings, a limitation recorded in Supplementary Section S3. Accordingly, these covariates are interpreted as properties of the text on an adult referent, not as what a child felt. The variability of valence and of arousal, and the additive and temporal connective densities, will be computed for description only and excluded from the component solution. The generated-or-classic indicator enters as a covariate, and the substantive comparison between generated and classic texts is a contingent hypothesis, as question (j) in @tbl-unresolved explains. Because predictors are standardised within language, a pooled coefficient averages slopes expressed in each language's own standard-deviation units. We will report the raw-scale standard deviation of each component per language so that coefficients can be converted to raw units, and the language-varying slopes summarise the heterogeneity this induces.

The age band is the platform's record of the child's age group, reduced to the two bands this study covers. The data controller's answer to question (h) is that the band is derived from the age a family gave when it created the child's profile, so it is family-reported and unverified. Unless a family updates it, a band set long before the window may understate the child's age at the time of reading. An account whose recorded band changes within the window contributes each session under the band recorded for it, and the number of such accounts will be reported. The reading level is the level the family has set for the session, which determines which version of a text is served. Narration is the session-level narration flag, which records whether narration was switched on at the end of the session. Under the rule registered for that answer to question (a), the variable is treated as narration availability, and the Hypothesis 4 contrast is an intention-to-treat comparison.

Accumulated in-app reading, which serves Hypothesis 6, is the cumulative count of words in completed distinct stories the account read before the current session. It is expressed in story units, each story's word count being divided by the median word count of the distinct texts with eligible readings in its language. Entering it as $\log(1 + \text{accumulated stories})$ keeps it defined at the first eligible session, where the count is zero. On a raw word count, the logarithm would jump after a child's first session and change little afterwards. The within-child term would then mostly contrast that session, when the app was still new to the child, with later ones.

The transformed variable is decomposed into the account's mean and the current session's deviation from it. Both parts are divided by one constant per language, the root mean square of the deviations over that language's tier-2 readings. The registered coefficient is then the change in the standardised outcome per within-child standard deviation of accumulated reading, the unit the design analysis simulated (Supplementary Section S5). Scaling a within-person effect by within-person variation keeps differences between children's means out of its unit [@schuurmanHowCompareCrosslagged2016]. The constant is pooled over children because standardising by each child's own standard deviation needs far more readings than the three that admit a child to tier 2 [@wangStandardizingWithinpersonEffects2019]. With both parts on the same scale, the difference between their coefficients remains a contextual effect. The logarithm of session order, the days since the account's previous eligible session and the days since its first eligible session enter the tier-2 model with the two terms.

The data are crossed: each reading belongs to one account, but a text is met by many accounts and exists in several languages and at several reading levels. An account may read in more than one language. We will treat Account, Text, Language, Country and App version as crossed grouping factors and report the counts supporting each before fitting any model. The grouping-factor rule admits a factor other than Text and Account when it has at least five levels with at least 20 eligible readings each. Otherwise, the factor is dropped, and the omission will be reported. Reading level, with only three levels, enters as a fixed factor. If at least 90 per cent of texts are read in only one eligible session, a Text varying intercept is not estimable and is replaced by varying intercepts for the repeated attribute combination that generated the text. These thresholds are registered conventions, and any consequence of them will be reported.

### Randomisation and blinding

Nothing in this study is randomised, and no allocation, assignment or condition is under anyone's control.

Data collection and analysis will not be performed blind to the conditions of the study. The platform collects the data without researcher involvement. Before in-principle acceptance, however, we are blind to the outcome in the extract, which the data controller holds as described under Data provenance, sequestration and outcome blindness. After transfer, analysis will not be blind to the values of the predictors or grouping variables, since the models require them. We will write, run and debug the outcome-model code against data simulated from the design specification deposited with this protocol, so that every script is complete and tested before we receive the real extract.

## Sampling plan

The sample is a census. We will analyse every eligible record in one frozen extract, whose closing date is fixed before any outcome model is fitted, with no sequential testing or optional stopping.

We will first exclude sessions the platform flags as incomplete or crashed, duplicated event records, accounts the platform flags as duplicates and stories without a positive word count.

Two nested samples are drawn from the remaining records, tier 1 for the text hypotheses and tier 2 for the within-child hypothesis, because these hypotheses are identified at different levels. Tier 1 comprises every completed reading whose account is recorded in either age band (7 to 8, or 9 and over) and whose reading language the feature pipeline covers. The story text must have been supplied, and the reading time must fall inside the plausibility bounds below. Where an account read the same text more than once, only the first reading enters tier 1. Repeated readings are retained for the practice analysis under Sensitivity analyses. The unit of analysis is one reading of one text by one account.

Under the Account rule, Account receives a varying intercept if at least 10 per cent of tier-1 readings come from accounts contributing two or more readings. If fewer do, the intercept cannot be separated from residual variance and is dropped. The sample's reduced effective independence is then stated with every tier-1 interval. The threshold is a registered convention. It is applied before anything is fitted, to the tier-1 sample as counted in the audit of the frozen extract. The provider-computed counts of sessions per account are not used for it, because they apply no tier-1 exclusion except the restriction to the two age bands.

Tier 2 comprises the tier-1 accounts contributing at least three eligible readings of distinct texts. Three is the smallest number that leaves a degree of freedom once a within-child slope and an intercept are estimated.

The plausibility bounds on reading time per word are set by what a child could physically be doing, not by these data. We will exclude a reading faster than 400 words per minute (0.15 seconds per word) as too fast to be reading. Silent reading in educated adults typically runs between 200 and 400 words per minute [@raynerSoMuchRead2016], so a child of 7 to 11 sustaining more than 400 is not plausibly reading every word. A meta-analysis of Spanish reading rates applied the same cut, treating rates above it as a sign that the reader had skipped part of the text. It removed 313 cases, all of them silent-reading rates, from tests that assessed 19,237 participants [@ripollsalcedaReadingRateSpanish2020]. A reading slower than 10 words per minute (six seconds per word) will be excluded as a story left open. The slow bound lies below the meta-analysis's slowest pooled mean, 30 words per minute for Spanish first graders reading silently, though above the normal-range floor proposed for that grade, 8 words per minute. We will report the number and proportion removed under each rule, by language, age band, reading level and narration state.

If the provider-computed counts show more than 1 per cent of sessions sharing one value of recorded reading time, we will locate that value in the transferred extract before fitting any outcome model. We will treat it as a right-censoring point if it lies in the upper decile of recorded reading times. If so, the reading-time models will use a censored lognormal likelihood, with those sessions retained as censored.

No excluded datum is replaced. A participant-flow diagram will report every exclusion and the retained accounts, readings and texts, overall and by language.

### Measurement, availability and missingness audit

Digital traces have an error taxonomy distinct from that of surveys [@senTotalErrorFramework2021], and four concerns here fall under the types it names. Three are trace measurement errors, in which the platform's record is an imperfect proxy for the construct. They concern the age-band and reading-level categories, instrument drift as the app changes version and a reading-time interval that is not fully documented, the subject of question (c) in @tbl-unresolved. That drift is also a change in platform affordances, which the taxonomy treats as a separate type. The fourth concern is a trace selection error, since a session that is closed or times out before its last page is not in the extract. A completed reading whose recorded time was capped by a timeout is instead censored, and the censoring rule above applies.

Before fitting any outcome model, we will run and archive an audit of the frozen extract and its dictionary. The audit establishes field availability and units, the granularity of the age field, the intervals between an account's sessions and, crossed with no other field, the proportions of the three rating categories. It records how often texts and reading levels recur, how many accounts change reading level within the window and how the narration flag behaves within accounts and sessions. Its checks cover duplicate and crash flags, changes across app versions, per-language feature coverage and every nesting and crossing count the models require. Missingness will be reported for every planned variable, overall and by language, age band, reading level, narration state and session order.

A feature structurally unavailable in a language is not imputed, so the language does not contribute it. A session missing an outcome is excluded from the model for that outcome alone, and a missing narration flag does not remove a session from a model without a narration term. No variable is selected, transformed or discarded because of its association with reading time or the rating.

The Hypothesis 5 rating is optional and was present in only 10 of the structural sample's 35 sessions, so we expect high missingness.
