If the rating is missing for more than 5 per cent of otherwise eligible sessions, we will model its availability from observed pre-response variables. In that case, we will report an inverse-probability-weighted analysis as a sensitivity check, showing its weight distributions and common support.

### Design and precision analysis

Nature Human Behaviour's guidelines set 0.95 as the a priori power floor for frequentist plans. For inference by Bayes factors, they require either data collection until the Bayes factor reaches 10 in one direction or the other, or a maximum feasible sample at which an inconclusive result would still be an important message for the field. This study uses an estimation design on a census of existing records, so the second provision applies. With no further data to collect, the frozen extract is the maximum feasible sample. The design nonetheless takes its evidence threshold from the first provision. As Decision rules sets out, a non-negligible verdict requires an interval Bayes factor of at least 10 under the reference prior, the weakly informative prior registered under Priors. The assurance level at which a hypothesis counts as adequately powered is registered as 0.90, with every 0.95 requirement reported from the same archived curves (Supplementary Section S5). A hypothesis declared underpowered is still fitted and reported, so its interval bounds the effect even where it cannot decide the hypothesis. The assurance analysis is the fixed-sample counterpart of a Bayes factor design analysis [@schonbrodtBayesFactorDesign2018].

The text coefficients are identified between distinct texts, so their precision depends on how many the extract contains, a number not yet known. To find how many are needed, we simulated data with pilotr from the deposited design specifications [@bernabeuPilotr2026]. The texts sweep varied the number of distinct texts at an average of twelve readings per text, the readings sweep varied readings per text at 250 texts and the tier-2 sweep varied the number of children. The simulated tier-1 model contained the three components, the age band, the two age-band interactions and a text intercept. The narration model contained the lexical and continuity components, the narration flag, their interactions with it and a text intercept. The tier-2 model had the three components, a single accumulated-reading trend and child and text intercepts, without the age band or its interactions. In the generated reading times, the text intercept contributed 9 per cent of the variance, the child intercept 20 per cent and the residual the remainder. These shares are assumptions, set before any reading time from this platform could be linked to a text, since no estimate of them exists for this app. The text share matters most for the requirements, and it lies just below published decompositions of children's reading rates over many passages. Those put the variance between passages at about 10 to 13 per cent [@poncyInvestigationReliabilityStandard2005; @barthEffectsStudentText2014; @francisExtendingSimpleView2018], and at 13 per cent in the logs of a shared-reading app [@wangMonitoringOralReading2024]. In tier 1, each simulated account contributed one reading, so the child variance reached the fitted model as residual variance, and how the remainder divides between child and residual cannot change a simulated tier-1 requirement. The same decompositions put most of the variance between readers, 81 per cent in @poncyInvestigationReliabilityStandard2005. A child share that large would lower the tier-2 requirement, but readings in an unsupervised app are likely to be noisier than assessment readings, so the registered 20 per cent is the cautious choice. Supplementary Section S5 reports the tier-1 requirements re-derived with the text share at 5, 13 and 20 per cent. Over that range, a main effect needed between about 490 and 1,240 distinct texts for a determinate verdict nine times in ten, whereas the interactions needed between about 1,140 and 1,500 and changed little.

Data were simulated on the within-language standardised scale, so a simulated coefficient is directly comparable with the region of practical equivalence. The region's half-width, 0.05 standard deviations, is a registered convention and the smallest effect this protocol treats as worth reporting. The simulated effect of 0.10 standard deviations, a second registered convention, is twice the half-width, because an effect at the boundary cannot be declared outside the region. A null condition with every coefficient set to zero established how reliably the design can declare practical equivalence and how often it declares a zero effect non-negligible.

The simulated models are simpler than the registered ones, and the simplifications bias the requirements in different directions. They omit the narration terms of the tier-1 model, the reading-level adjustment, the covariates, the language, country and app-version intercepts, the language-varying slopes, the distributional sub-model and the review-derived priors. The simulation generated child variance but analysed a dataset in which each account contributes one reading, so this variance entered the fitted model as inflated residual variance. In that one respect, the requirements below for the reading-time models are upper bounds. In the ordinal model for Hypothesis 5, the unmodelled variance also attenuates every coefficient towards zero, so the projection in Supplementary Section S5 starts from the attenuated estimate and is not an upper bound. Adjusting for reading level, which moves all three feature families together, will remove some of the components' variance and raise every requirement, whereas the language-varying slopes and the priors will lower them. The prevalence-weighted main effects have the precision of the pooled slope and no design effect, but each interaction incurs the design effect for imbalance applied by the first two adjustments below. When the design analysis is re-run at the observed inputs, we will refit one grid point of each sweep with the registered brms specification, compute both registered criteria from those posteriors and report the difference.

The simulation scored its verdicts by criteria that lie between the registered posterior and Bayes-factor criteria. It counted a verdict as determinate when the 95 per cent interval lay wholly outside the region, and as equivalence when it lay wholly inside. An interval wholly outside the region leaves at most 2.5 per cent of a symmetric posterior inside it, whereas the posterior criterion allows up to 5 per cent. An interval wholly inside the region guarantees at least 95 per cent of the posterior inside it, which is the registered equivalence criterion.

For a non-negligible verdict, the Bayes-factor criterion is stricter than either the posterior criterion or the simulation's, so it sets the requirement. Under the reference prior, the interval Bayes factor against the region reaches 10 when the posterior mass inside it falls to 0.8 per cent for a main effect and 1.7 per cent for an interaction. For a normal posterior, those masses place the estimate 2.42 and 2.13 standard errors beyond the region's edge, against the interval's 1.96. The requirements under this criterion were computed from the same archived curves by that normal approximation, using the deposited script `design_analysis/solve_at_bf10.R` (checked against the simulation in Supplementary Section S5). The re-run at the observed inputs will compute this criterion by simulation from the brms refits and supersede these approximations.

Pairing the two criteria combines Bayesian estimation with Bayes-factor testing. These approaches differ in whether the model privileges a theoretically useful value such as the null, and each serves a different goal [@rouderBayesianInferencePsychology2018]. With the same region and prior, though, the interval Bayes factor and the posterior odds of the region come from one posterior and differ only in whether the prior odds are divided out [@campbellBayesFactorsPosterior2023]. Calibrated to the same error rate, the interval Bayes factor, the posterior rule and the frequentist equivalence test make almost the same decisions [@lindeDecisionsAboutEquivalence2023; @campbellReLindeEt2021]. The choice between the two criteria therefore turns on which verdict each should decide, and reporting both is the current recommendation for inferences about null and non-null effects [@lakensImprovingInferencesAbout2020; @heckReviewApplicationsBayes2023]. The posterior rule has an independent decision-theoretic justification [@kelterDecisionTheoreticFoundations2025].

For the three text coefficients (@fig-precision, panel a), an effect of 0.10 standard deviations reached a determinate verdict nine times in ten at 738 distinct texts for lexical difficulty (95 per cent interval 640 to 843). Grammatical load needed 660 (593 to 731) and referential continuity 634 (568 to 704). At 0.95, the three coefficients needed 926, 812 and 784. The age-band interactions needed about twice as many: 1,230 texts for grammatical load (1,107 to 1,359) and 1,431 for referential continuity (1,276 to 1,596) at 0.90. At 0.95, the grammatical-load interaction needed 1,510 texts, and the continuity interaction did not reach that target within the 1,600 texts simulated. The narration contrast needed 1,234 texts (1,113 to 1,361) before the design effect for imbalance is applied, and 1,506 at 0.95. That requirement applies to the lexical-by-narration interaction coefficient. It is a lower bound for the difference-of-proportions rule of Hypothesis 4, because that rule's draw-by-draw ratio has heavier tails than the coefficient it is built from. Declaring practical equivalence when the true effect was zero required a similar number of texts. A main effect was correctly declared equivalent in 87 to 90 per cent of replicates at 800 texts and in every one at 1,600, but the interactions reached 89 to 92 per cent only at 1,600. An inconclusive verdict is therefore predictable from the number of texts alone. A zero main effect or age-band interaction was wrongly declared non-negligible in at most 2 of 120 replicates (1.7 per cent) at every grid point, from 50 to 1,600 texts.

For the unadjusted trend, the within-child term needed 609 children in tier 2 (528 to 697), each reading five distinct texts, and 731 (621 to 851) at 0.95. The registered term is adjusted for the three covariates defined under Measures. Session order and the time since the first session are correlated with accumulated reading within a child, so the unadjusted figure understates the requirement. The tier-2 re-run below re-derives it with all three.

Under the Bayes-factor criterion, the requirements for a non-negligible verdict rise. The three main effects need about 930 distinct texts for lexical difficulty, 930 for grammatical load and 940 for referential continuity at 0.90, and 1,120, 1,120 and 1,130 at 0.95. The grammatical-load interaction needs about 1,470 texts and the continuity interaction 1,480 at 0.90, neither reaching 0.95 within the 1,600 texts simulated. The narration interaction needs about 1,470 texts at 0.90, before the design effect for imbalance, and likewise does not reach 0.95 within 1,600. Tier 2 needs about 810 children at 0.90 and 970 at 0.95.

In the readings sweep, raising readings per text from 2 to 60 (@fig-precision, panel b) narrowed the interval on a main effect from 0.19 to 0.08 standard deviations. Even so, a main effect's probability of a determinate verdict rose no higher than 0.70. Over the same range, that probability for the age-band interactions climbed from under 0.11 to between 0.87 and 0.90. Sessions and texts are therefore not interchangeable. A text coefficient is bounded by how many different texts the extract contains, whereas an interaction between a text property and a reader attribute gains from many different children meeting the same text.

The threshold each hypothesis has to clear is recorded in @tbl-design and fixed before any part of the extract is transferred. Seven registered adjustments of the design analysis each draw on the provider-computed counts, the audit of the frozen extract or the archived output of the prior-derivation pipeline. The first two are analytic corrections for imbalance. The simulation balanced the narration contrast, but narration was on in 32 of the 35 sessions of the structural sample. An unbalanced binary contrast at prevalence $p$ inflates the variance of its interaction coefficient by $1/(4p(1-p))$ relative to balance. The first adjustment multiplies the simulated Hypothesis 4 requirement by that factor at the observed narration prevalence, about 3.0 at a prevalence of 0.91, and states the adjusted requirement before fitting. The second applies the same factor to the Hypothesis 2 and 3 requirements at the observed age-band prevalence, since the simulation balanced the bands as well. The third re-runs the rating simulation at the rating availability and text reuse in the provider-computed counts. The fourth re-runs it at the observed proportions of the three rating categories. Because the counts report only how often a rating is present, these proportions are tabulated from the transferred extract before fitting, without reference to any text or reader attribute. The values published for an earlier window of this platform [@ratnerProductiveStruggleChildrens2026] cover ages from three years below this study's younger band, so they are not used as inputs. The fifth re-runs the tier-2 sweep at the observed distribution of sessions per child. For that re-run alone, we will add the three registered covariates to the deposited tier-2 specification, with every term entered as Measures specifies. The simulated sessions will be spaced as in the extract, and story lengths will be generated so that accumulated reading correlates with session order as it does there. The extended specification will be deposited before it is run. The thresholds these three re-runs yield replace the ones in @tbl-design for the underpowered declarations of Hypotheses 5 and 6.

The sixth adjustment depends on the output of the prior-derivation pipeline (Supplementary Section S6). Before any outcome datum is accessed, we will record from that output whether the absolute value of each component's pooled estimate on the model's scale exceeds 0.10 standard deviations. Where that absolute value lies between 0.05 and 0.10, the texts sweep will be re-simulated with the deposited scripts at that value in place of the 0.10 input. The resulting threshold replaces the one in @tbl-design for that component before fitting. If it lies at or below the region's half-width, no number of texts could yield a determinate verdict at that size. The 0.10 convention is then retained, and the discrepancy will be reported with the component's verdict. The seventh adjustment runs only if the compression diagnostic falls below its cut-off. It re-runs the texts sweep at the observed number of unnarrated readings per text, taken from the audit, and yields the threshold for the narration rule stated with Hypothesis 1. That threshold is stated before any Hypothesis 1 verdict is taken from an unnarrated slope.

## Analysis plan

We will fit all confirmatory models as Bayesian hierarchical models with the brms package and its Stan backend [@burknerBrmsPackageBayesian2017]. Continuous predictors will be standardised within language after transformation, except accumulated reading, whose scaling by within-child variation is set out under Measures. Where the accompanying systematic review supports it, weakly informative priors will be replaced by review-derived priors, as described under Priors.

### Outcome-blind dimension reduction

The observed text features are correlated because the reading level a text is written for moves lexical, grammatical and discourse properties together. We will reduce them by principal component analysis, separately within the lexical, grammatical and discourse families, without treating them as effects of an unobserved latent cause [@crossleyDevelopingLinguisticConstructs2025]. The affective measures will be kept as separate secondary predictors, because valence and arousal are theoretically distinct and need not move together. Narrativity, though computed as a discourse feature, will likewise be excluded from the component solution.

Each distinct text will contribute one row however often it was read, so a popular text does not determine the solution. Within a family, a text enters the solution only if it has valid values on every retained feature. A text with fewer than five sentences, as segmented under Materials, enters no family's solution. The theory object records this minimum as the boundary condition for referential continuity. Since the tier-1 model includes all three components, a text below the minimum contributes to no confirmatory model, so the thresholds in @tbl-design apply to the distinct-text counts that remain. We will report, per language, the distribution of sentences and of words per text and the number of texts the minimum removes.

Counts will be transformed with $\log(1+x)$ and bounded proportions with an empirical-logit transform where these reduce skew. A feature is dropped from a language if more than 20 per cent of its values are missing or its standard deviation after transformation is below 0.01. The text-coverage rule drops a feature from any language in which fewer than 80 per cent of texts receive a valid token-level match. A language contributes to a family's solution only if it has at least 100 distinct eligible texts and at least three valid features in that family, two of them anchors (defined below). Where two features correlate at $|r| > .90$, the retained one is chosen in this order: lower missingness, then broader language coverage, then higher extraction reliability on a manually checked sample, then the measure listed first under Materials. No outcome correlation enters any of these decisions.

To stop the largest language determining the solution, we will compute a correlation matrix within each eligible language, transform the correlations to Fisher's *z* and average them with equal weight per language. The average will then be transformed back for analysis [@revelleRPackagePsych2023]. Sampling adequacy requires individual Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin values above .50 and an overall value above .60. Parallel analysis [@hornRationaleTestNumber1965] will set the number of components, retaining each component whose eigenvalue exceeds the 95th percentile of the corresponding eigenvalues from 10,000 random datasets. That percentile criterion, Glorfeld's modification of Horn's average [@glorfeldImprovementHornParallel1995], is the more conservative of the two. The scree plot will be reported but will not override that rule. Where a family retains more than one component, the components will be rotated obliquely with promax, because linguistic properties co-occur and do not vary independently [@biberVariationSpeechWriting1988]. Promax will use $\kappa$ = 4, the default of the implementation used [@revelleRPackagePsych2023]. We will then apply the regression scoring coefficients from the frozen, language-balanced solution to each text's features, standardised within language.

The anchors of each confirmatory component are the features that identify it. For LexicalDifficulty, they are frequency, surprisal and word length. Surprisal is grouped with the lexical features because it is hardest to separate from word frequency at the word level [@ohDissociableFrequencyEffects2025]. Model surprisal also diverges most from human reading times on the rarest words [@ohFrequencyExplainsInverse2024]. The correlation between surprisal and each grammatical feature will be reported per language next to the pattern matrix, but the family assignment fixed here does not depend on it. For GrammaticalLoad, the anchors are dependency distance, subordination, clause density, sentence length and noun-phrase depth. For ReferentialContinuity, they are adjacent-sentence similarity, referential overlap and the densities of causal and contrastive connectives. The additive and temporal densities are descriptive only, as stated under Measures, because causal and contrastive connectives raised comprehension, temporal ones had no effect and additive ones lowered it [@kleijnComprehensionEffectsConnectives2019]. A count mixing all connective types therefore has no defined expected sign. Each component's sign is set to match the orientation stated in the Introduction.

Under the construction rule, each confirmatory component must load at least .30 in absolute value on at least two of its anchors. If no component in a family meets this rule, the hypotheses resting on that family are reported as untestable. Where more than one component meets the rule, the one with the most anchors reaching the .30 threshold is confirmatory, and the others are reported descriptively. In the discourse family, a tie is broken in favour of the component on which the causal and contrastive densities load highest, because the cue-utilisation account that Hypothesis 3 adjudicates is stated for connectives. The tie-break, a registered convention, implies no claim that connectives are the more predictive cue, since in the child sample closest to this one, deep and referential cohesion both explained unique variance in comprehension [@pickrenContributionTextCharacteristics2022]. If the component so chosen loads below .30 on both connective densities, Hypothesis 3 is still tested on it, under the narrower interpretation given in @tbl-design.

Concreteness and age of acquisition come from native norms, which measure them differently in each language. They are therefore not anchors and enter the language-specific solutions but not the pooled one. In a sensitivity analysis, we will add both to the pooled lexical solution, averaging each feature's correlations over the languages that retain it. We will report that solution with Tucker's congruence coefficient between its loadings and those of the primary solution. Every congruence coefficient in this protocol will be computed over the features that both solutions contain.

The component solution will be reported in full: the pattern matrix, the component correlations, the variance explained, the language-specific matrices, the loading congruence for the five largest languages and the raw-scale standard deviation of mean dependency distance per language. Language-specific and sparse solutions are sensitivity analyses and will never replace the primary solution after an outcome is seen.

### Confirmatory models

In tier 1, we will estimate a model of within-language standardised log reading time per word. Its fixed effects are the three components, the age band, the narration flag, each component's interactions with the age band and with narration, the reading level, log text length, narrativity, valence, arousal and the generated-or-classic indicator. The age band and narration are coded as deviations from their observed prevalence. The model has varying intercepts for Text, Country and App version, and varying intercepts and uncorrelated component slopes for Language. Under the working assumption stated under Materials, it also has a varying intercept for the underlying story, crossed with Language, which question (d) in @tbl-unresolved can remove. Account receives a varying intercept where the Account rule under Sampling plan is met. Hypotheses 1 to 4 will be evaluated in this model. Because the model includes every component-by-age-band and component-by-narration interaction, each registered interaction is adjusted for the others, and each main effect is the prevalence-weighted average slope defined in the Introduction. A component's slope in a given state is recovered draw by draw as the main effect plus the interaction multiplied by that state's deviation score. LexicalDifficulty × AgeBand enters no registered test and will not be taken as evidence about whether the age band stands in for a bundle of developing capacities. The three component-by-narration terms enter a registered test only through the state-specific slopes, the lexical and continuity terms through the Hypothesis 4 contrast and all three through the narration rule stated with Hypothesis 1. All four terms will be reported with posterior medians and intervals, so that no term is reported selectively.

The Hypothesis 4 contrast is computed from these state-specific slopes. For each posterior draw, the proportional attenuation of a component is one minus its narrated slope divided by its unnarrated slope, so a positive value means a smaller coefficient under narration. The contrast is computed only under the Hypothesis 4 precondition, which requires fewer than 5 per cent of the draws of each derived unnarrated slope to lie inside the region. The confidence interval for a ratio of two normally distributed estimates is bounded only when its denominator differs significantly from zero [@fiellerProblemsIntervalEstimation1954; @vonluxburgGeometricApproachConfidence2009]. The precondition asks the same of the posterior draws, with the region in place of zero, and makes no claim that either slope is an effect, so the Bayes-factor criterion does not apply. Draws in which either unnarrated slope lies inside the region will be excluded from the ratio, and their fraction reported. As a sensitivity analysis, the contrast will be repeated with a fixed denominator, each narration interaction divided by the posterior median of its unnarrated slope, and reported with the draw-by-draw version.

The first of three further rules for Hypothesis 4 concerns accounts observed in both narration states. If they cover at least as many distinct texts as the adjusted requirement, the within-account contrast restricted to them becomes the primary estimate, and the full-sample contrast is reported with it. If they cover fewer, the within-account contrast remains a sensitivity analysis, and selection into narration state is acknowledged wherever the full-sample estimate is reported.

Second, the tier-1 model contains a distributional sub-model in which the narration flag also predicts the residual standard deviation. The ratio of the narrated to the unnarrated residual standard deviation is the compression diagnostic. A ratio below 0.5 is the registered signature of the audio setting the pace. When the diagnostic falls below that threshold, the full-sample verdict is withheld and Hypothesis 4 is evaluated in the subset described next. For each language, we will report the share of narrated sessions whose rate lies within 10 per cent of that language's median narrated rate, because the ratio can miss a minority of audio-paced sessions. The share enters no decision rule.

Third, the contrast will be repeated in the narrated sessions the audio cannot have paced. For each language, the narration rate will be estimated as the median words per minute of its narrated sessions, and a narrated session counts as unpaced when its rate exceeds 1.5 times that median. Where a language has fewer than 100 narrated sessions, a fixed bound applies instead. The bound is that language's adult read-aloud mean in the International Reading Speed Texts or, for a language they do not cover, the slowest of their 17 means, 138 words per minute for Arabic [@trauzettelklosinskiStandardizedAssessmentReading2012]. The premise is that narration produced for children is paced no faster than adult oral reading in the same language. If Korean has fewer than 100 narrated sessions, the fixed bound classes fewer of its sessions as unpaced, for the reason given under Measures, and the size of this conservative subset will be reported. Pacing does not explain selectivity that persists in the unpaced subset. Hypothesis 4 is reported as underpowered from the subset if the subset contains fewer distinct texts than the adjusted requirement. If the data controller supplies the audio's duration for every eligible text, or discloses a fixed narration rate, that quantity replaces the median estimate and the fixed bound, and the substitution will be reported. A narrated session then counts as unpaced when its rate exceeds 1.5 times the rate the audio implies. A duration supplied for only some texts defines the unpaced subset among those texts in a sensitivity analysis.

The Hypothesis 5 model will have the same fixed and grouping structure and a cumulative-logit likelihood over the three rating categories, with category thresholds that vary by language. Cross-language differences in use of the middle category are then not mistaken for differences in text difficulty. Whether the Account intercept is estimable in this model depends on how many accounts contribute more than one rated reading, which the tier-1 count does not establish. We will report that number and, where the intercept is not estimable, acknowledge child-level scale use as a limit on the rating. Band-specific odds ratios, derived from the component-by-age-band terms, will be reported descriptively alongside the pooled ones. A text rated by fewer than five distinct children does not contribute, and the primary model is complete-case, with the inverse-probability sensitivity analysis registered under the audit.

For tier 2, we will refit the same specification with a varying intercept for Account and decompose accumulated reading into the account's mean and the current session's deviation from it [@curranDisaggregationWithinpersonBetweenperson2011]. Both parts enter with the three covariates set out under Measures, and the deviation term tests Hypothesis 6.

Posterior predictive checks will assess calibration and residual structure by language, age band, reading level and narration state in every model.

### Priors

Priors for the main effects of the three components on reading time will be derived from the systematic review by a deterministic pipeline. A derived prior requires at least two independent papers in the review reporting a standardised regression coefficient for the component. The pipeline's frozen rules translate a pooled estimate to the model's scale only for reading time and for accuracy. The rating coefficients of Hypothesis 5, on a cumulative-logit scale, and the within-child coefficient of Hypothesis 6 therefore keep weakly informative priors. The pooled estimates the pipeline writes for them will be reported beside their posteriors. The rules were first committed in August 2026 and last revised on 16 September 2026, while the review's tables of extracted records and effects held no data rows. They are deposited with this protocol, and Supplementary Section S6 summarises them and records the test extractions that preceded them. The pipeline will be run before any outcome datum is accessed. The review's estimates for the corresponding predictor family and outcome class will be sign-harmonised to the direction in which each component is scored, so that slower reading carries the same sign in every estimate. They will be kept within compatible metric families and pooled by random-effects meta-analysis, with one estimate per paper per relation. The prior is Student's $t(3, \hat\mu, \sigma)$, where $\hat\mu$ is the pooled estimate translated to the model's scale and $\sigma$ is twice the combined pooling and between-paper uncertainty, with a floor of 0.10. The doubling and the floor allow for the gap between measures taken in the laboratory and passively timed reading in an app.

The same review motivates the hypotheses, so the evidence that generates a prediction also centres its prior. Two features of the decision rule keep that from being circular. First, the verdict's posterior criterion is evaluated on the derived-prior fit, but its evidence criterion, the interval Bayes factor defined under Decision rules, is computed from the weakly informative refit described next. A prior centred in the predicted direction therefore does not supply the evidence that confirms the prediction. Second, a hypothesis whose verdict changes under the weakly informative refit is reported as sensitive to the prior, and its result is not counted as conclusive. We will report prior-data conflict diagnostics for every review-derived prior.

Every main effect and interaction without a review-derived prior keeps a weakly informative prior, $t(3, 0, 0.5)$ for a standardised main effect and $t(3, 0, 0.25)$ for an interaction. That covers every interaction term, the main effects of narration and the age band, the coefficients of Hypotheses 5 and 6, every secondary predictor and covariate, and any component main effect with fewer than two such papers. Group-level and residual standard deviations take half-$t(3, 0, 1)$ priors, and any estimated correlation matrix takes LKJ($\eta$ = 2) [@lewandowskiGeneratingRandomCorrelation2009]. Intercept priors will be calibrated by prior-predictive simulation to the outcome scale, without reference to any predictor-outcome association. The full prior table and its forest plots will be archived before the extract is transferred and will accompany the Stage 2 report. If the review's extraction has not produced the table within the four weeks expected under Timeline, the transfer will wait for it for up to three months after in-principle acceptance. If the table is still missing then, the weakly informative priors will be primary and the pipeline will not be run, and either the delay or the change will be reported. We will refit every model with weakly informative priors throughout and with the derived scales halved and doubled. Where a meta-analysis in the review subsumes other papers in it, every model whose priors it informs will also be refitted with priors from the alternative pooling described in Supplementary Section S6. Conclusions will be reported under each refit.

### Decision rules and diagnostics

For every confirmatory coefficient, we will report the posterior median, the 95 per cent highest-density interval, the probability of the predicted direction, the posterior proportion inside the region of practical equivalence and a model-implied contrast on an interpretable scale. The region is $|\beta| < 0.05$ standard deviations for a one-standard-deviation change in a predictor of reading time, and a half-width of log(1.05) on the log-odds scale for the rating model. More than 95 per cent of the posterior inside the region counts as practical equivalence. A practically non-negligible association is labelled in the predicted or opposite direction by the sign of the posterior median. It requires less than 5 per cent of the posterior inside the region and an interval Bayes factor of at least 10 for the region on that side against the region inside. Any other result is inconclusive.

The Bayes factor is the ratio of the posterior odds of the two regions to their prior odds [@klugkistBayesianModelSelection2005; @moreyBayesFactorApproaches2011; @hoijtinkTutorialTestingHypotheses2019]. The posterior odds come from the draws of the weakly informative refit, whose Student-*t* prior is the reference prior for evidence. The prior odds come from that prior's mass in the region, known in closed form. No marginal likelihood is needed, so the Bayes factor avoids the fragility that marginal-likelihood Bayes factors show in mixed models [@vandoornBayesFactorsMixed2023; @schadHowAccurateAre2026]. For the two-sided interactions of Hypotheses 2 and 3, it is computed for each side against the region, and the verdict states the side the evidence favours. Every Bayes factor is reported alongside its verdict, with its values under the derived priors and their halved and doubled scales, from the refits registered under Priors.

Which of the two criteria is stricter depends on the kind of verdict. Under the reference prior, 95 per cent of the posterior outside the region corresponds to a Bayes factor of only 1.5 for a main effect and 3.2 for an interaction. These values are low because the prior already places most of its mass outside the region, so the Bayes factor decides non-negligibility. For equivalence, 95 per cent inside corresponds to a Bayes factor above 100 for the region. A Bayes factor of 10 alone, by contrast, would be reached with less than half of the posterior inside it, so the posterior mass decides equivalence [@kruschkeRejectingAcceptingParameter2018]. Taking the stricter criterion for each kind of verdict keeps the journal's evidence threshold for Bayes factors without letting a diffuse prior produce an equivalence verdict.

The same two criteria apply to the Hypothesis 5 odds ratios on the log-odds scale. For the Hypothesis 5 ordering clause, a posterior probability of at least 0.90 that the three coefficients rank as they do for reading time counts as agreement on order, and anything lower as order not established. The Hypothesis 4 contrast, a derived quantity, is judged by three posterior criteria. They are at least 95 per cent of the posterior of the difference of attenuations above 0.20, more than 95 per cent inside the region and more than 95 per cent below -0.05. @tbl-design gives the interpretation of each outcome, and a posterior meeting none of the criteria is inconclusive. We will report the interval Bayes factors of the contrast's two constituent narration interactions. The fixed-denominator sensitivity contrast is evaluated against the same thresholds.

Each hypothesis is a single registered test with its own decision rule, and no claim aggregates evidence across hypotheses, so no correction for multiple comparisons will be applied. The one composite claim, the combined Hypothesis 1 verdict, follows an intersection-union rule. It is recorded only when all three coefficients are individually non-negligible in the predicted direction, so its error rate cannot exceed that of any single component. Hierarchical shrinkage and the null condition of the design analysis, which reports how often a zero effect is wrongly declared non-negligible, calibrate the per-decision error rates behind @tbl-design.

Six registered contingencies depend on quantities computed after fitting, each a conditional rule stated where it applies. Two can leave a hypothesis without a verdict. Failure of the Hypothesis 4 precondition leaves Hypothesis 4 not evaluable, and failure of the positive control on recorded reading time leaves Hypotheses 1 to 4 and 6 not evaluable. Of the other four, the compression diagnostic, when it indicates compression, withholds the full-sample Hypothesis 4 verdict in favour of the unpaced subset. Under the narration rule stated with Hypothesis 1, the same diagnostic can move a component's Hypothesis 1 verdict to its derived unnarrated slope. Draws with an unnarrated slope inside the region are excluded from the Hypothesis 4 ratio. The third outcome-neutral check (next section) makes the within-level estimate primary for a component whose within-level coefficient falls below half its pooled magnitude. The prior-sensitivity rule above applies when a verdict changes under the weakly informative refit. Two further rules respond to the fitting itself and not to any estimated association. Models failing the sampling diagnostics are simplified in the order given below, and a failed permutation check withholds the confirmatory results until the source of the structure is found and reported.

We will run four chains of 4,000 iterations, half of them warm-up. Acceptable sampling requires $\hat{R}$ below 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes above 1,000 for every confirmatory parameter, no divergent transitions, satisfactory energy diagnostics and no unresolved maximum-treedepth warnings. Models failing these criteria will be refitted with a higher target acceptance rate, greater tree depth and more iterations. If simplification is still needed, every estimable varying intercept will be retained, and the language-level slopes will be removed in the fixed order continuity, then lexical, then grammatical. The model already omits the correlations among these slopes, the first parameters to drop when a random-effects structure is simplified [@barrRandomEffectsStructure2013; @matuschekBalancingTypeError2017]. The order follows the Introduction, which gives no reason for the continuity slope to vary across languages and expects the grammatical slope to vary most. Retaining that slope longest accords with advice to keep components expected on theoretical grounds [@matuschekBalancingTypeError2017]. We will report every simplification and its diagnostic consequence. Variance inflation factors will be reported for the fixed-effect design matrix, but a high value will not prompt an outcome-dependent deletion. The joint model remains primary, and single-family models will be reported as a collinearity sensitivity analysis.

For Hypotheses 2, 3 and 4, we will compare the model with one omitting the relevant interaction, using Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation. We will report the expected log pointwise predictive density difference, its standard error and the Pareto-$k$ diagnostics, with exact refits where importance sampling is unreliable. Predictive comparison supplements the coefficient-level summaries and decides no verdict.

### Outcome-neutral quality checks

Six checks are registered, each with a pass criterion and a consequence of failure. All but the fifth run before the confirmatory models are interpreted. The fifth, convergent validity, is the ordering clause of Hypothesis 5 and is evaluated with that hypothesis, which states the check's outcome if the hypothesis is underpowered. The first, second, fourth and sixth are decided without reference to any confirmatory coefficient, whereas the third is a robustness condition on the fitted text coefficients.

For the first check, a permutation null, we will reassign texts at random to readings within language and reading level, and refit the tier-1 model 200 times. The refits will use the maximum-likelihood analogue of that model, with the same fixed and estimable grouping structure. We choose this approximation because 200 full Bayesian refits are not feasible and the check concerns structure introduced by the pipeline. With no posterior or Bayes factor to evaluate, each refit is scored by the design analysis's criterion for a determinate verdict, a 95 per cent Wald interval wholly outside the region. No text coefficient may meet that criterion in more than 5 per cent of the refits. An inconclusive verdict on permuted data is expected at moderate text counts and is not a failure. Failure would mean the pipeline has introduced structure that does not come from the pairing of a text with a reading. In that case, we will withhold the confirmatory results until the source of that structure is found and reported.

The second check, a positive control on recorded reading time, requires total elapsed time to rise with the story's word count, with more than 99 per cent of the posterior above zero. Failure means recorded reading time does not index reading, and Hypotheses 1 to 4 and 6 are reported as not evaluable on this extract.

The third check asks whether the association is an artefact of platform assignment. We will re-estimate the three text coefficients separately within each reading level, and each must retain at least half its pooled magnitude. Where a coefficient falls short, the within-level estimate becomes primary for that component. The pooled estimate is then reported alongside it, and the assignment confound is named wherever the coefficient appears.

The fourth check tests three independence implications of the theory object. First, conditional on the reading level and the generated-or-classic indicator, the three components should be close to independent across texts. Second, narration should be unrelated to accumulated reading. Third, the difficulty rating should carry no further information about reading level once reading time is conditioned on. We will report each as an estimate with an interval. An implication fails when the 95 per cent interval of its conditional association lies entirely beyond 0.10 in standardised units. Such a failure does not invalidate the confirmatory tests and is reported as showing a path the causal graph omits. For the third implication, the omitted path would run directly to the reported difficulty from the reader's capacity, which the reading level partly indexes, or from the generation route. That path would be stated with the Hypothesis 5 odds ratios. Supplementary Section S1 gives the literature's reasons to expect this implication to fail, but the same criterion applies.

The sixth check validates the feature pipeline by hand. In a stratified random sample of 50 texts per language, we will inspect tokenisation, sentence splitting and dependency attachment, and report agreement per language before any feature is linked to outcome data. A native speaker of each language will adjudicate the sentence boundaries in 20 of these texts, and we will report how far the automatic sentence splits agree with that adjudication. A language whose labelled-attachment agreement with the hand-checked parse falls below .85 contributes to descriptive reporting but not to the grammatical component.

### Sensitivity analyses

Eight families of sensitivity analysis are registered here, all of them descriptive. Each bounds a primary estimate without replacing it, and none changes which hypothesis is tested or how its verdict is reached. Others are specified where they apply, among them the resource contrasts in Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 and the two refits registered with Hypothesis 6.

In the first family, we will refit the reading-time models with no plausibility bounds, with winsorisation at the 1st and 99th and at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles within language, and with posterior-predictive residual trimming. Where the censoring rule applies, we will report the censored and uncensored fits side by side. The tier-1 model will be refitted with the outcome per character, counted in the unit Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 use for word length (jamo in Korean, characters in Chinese and consonant and vowel letters in Thai), and its three component coefficients reported with the primary estimates.

The second family redefines eligibility, moving the tier-2 threshold from three distinct texts to two and to five and, as a practice analysis, adding repeated readings with a repetition indicator. With the sentence floor raised to eight, we will refit the tier-1 model and report its three component coefficients and distinct-text count with the primary estimates. Grouping by Text will be compared with grouping on the attribute combination that generated the text. The classic stories are likely to be public-domain texts, which the surprisal model's training corpus could contain (Supplementary Section S3). We will therefore report the mean per-word surprisal of classic and of generated texts per language before any outcome data are linked. For the same reason, we will refit the tier-1 model on generated texts alone, reporting its three component coefficients with the primary estimates.

The third family examines variation between languages, beginning with Hypothesis 6. Where Language, within tier 2, meets the grouping-factor rule under Measures, we will refit the tier-2 model with an uncorrelated language-varying slope on the accumulated-reading deviation and report the per-language slopes. If that refit fails the sampling diagnostics under Decision rules, it will be dropped and the drop reported. We will restrict analyses to the five largest languages and fit language-specific models and component solutions, reporting their loading congruence. From those fits, we will report the two age-band interactions per language next to the pooled coefficients, arranged by the orthographic depth assigned with Hypothesis 6. A further tier-1 refit will let both interactions vary by Language. The design analysis computed no requirement for the language-specific interactions or the language-varying refit, and both will give wide per-language posteriors. Neither supplies a second test of Hypothesis 2 or 3. The simplification order does not remove the language-varying interaction slopes, because they lie outside the tier-1 specification.

The fourth family asks how much the estimates depend on who is reading in which language. Before the transfer, we will deposit a lookup table marking whether each reading language is an official or majority language of each country, as a coarse indicator of the match between the two. We will report the cross-tabulation of reading language by account country and the number of accounts reading in more than one language. We will then refit the tier-1 model on sessions whose reading language is a language of the account's country. Its three component coefficients will be reported with the full-sample estimates, and its distinct-text count with the threshold in @tbl-design. The indicator enters no confirmatory model. Because it misclassifies in both directions, the refit bounds the estimates' sensitivity to sample composition and identifies no individual reader.

The fifth family rescores the text properties, replacing the component scores with sparse-component scores and with pre-specified equal-weight composites of the anchor features. For Hypothesis 3, we will report the age-band interaction of each ReferentialContinuity anchor from a model in which that anchor replaces the component, to check whether the four anchors agree in sign.

The sixth family varies the age contrast in Hypotheses 2 and 3. Where the audit finds the age field finer than two bands, we will re-estimate both age-band interactions with the finer age entered in two ways and report each coding's estimates with the two-band contrast. One coding treats the finer age as an ordinal monotonic predictor [@burknerModellingMonotonicEffects2020], the other as an unordered factor contrasting each finer band with the band for ages 7 to 8. Pages per hundred words, computed from the recorded page count, will enter a tier-1 refit along with its age-band interaction. The Hypothesis 2 and 3 interactions from that fit will be reported with the primary ones, to gauge how much of the age difference is time away from the text.

The seventh family adds analyses for Hypotheses 4 and 5. For narration, we will report the within-account contrast, where it is not already primary and can be formed, and the fixed-denominator contrast registered under Confirmatory models. We will also report the Hypothesis 4 contrast within each age band and the duration-adjusted contrast from a refit adding the spoken duration per word and its interaction with narration. Materials states when that duration is measured and when it is predicted. For the rating, we will compare the model under adjacent-category and cumulative-logit links, stratify it by language and set the inverse-probability analysis for rating non-response against the complete-case estimates.

Finally, the eighth family applies alternative regions of practical equivalence: 0.03 and 0.10 standard deviations for reading time, and half-widths of log(1.03) and log(1.10) on the log-odds scale for the rating. Interval Bayes factors will be recomputed for each region.

To ease comparison with earlier studies, we will report maximum-likelihood mixed models with the same fixed and estimable grouping structure in a supplementary table. They are descriptive and will decide no Bayesian verdict.

### Contingent hypotheses

Questions (j) and (m) bear on four further hypotheses. We specify them in full but outside the confirmatory set, because each depends on facts about the platform or the extract that have not yet been established.

A contingent hypothesis is activated only if its condition is established before submission. Facts about the platform require the data controller's written confirmation. The requirement that accounts be observed in both narration states is met if the provider-computed counts show any account that switched narration and the revised count script finds no account identifier in floating-point notation. Any record activating a hypothesis would be reproduced in Supplementary Section S7. At submission, no hypothesis has its full condition established, so none of the four is activated, as that section records. If a condition is established after submission, its hypothesis is reported at Stage 2 under Exploratory analyses and is not counted among the confirmatory tests. We retain the four hypotheses so that any such analysis is the one written before we had any access to the extract's outcome data. A hypothesis whose condition is never established is not run.

*C1: coherence and inferential comprehension.* Its condition is that item-level comprehension responses exist and include a recoverable question type. In an item-level model of response correctness, with inference questions coded 1 and literal questions 0, we would predict a positive ReferentialContinuity × QuestionType interaction. The association of continuity with correctness would then be larger where the question requires integration. We found no study that tests a continuity by question-type interaction directly. The prediction instead combines three results: an inference question is answered by integrating information across clauses [@freedAssessmentInferencemakingChildren2021], cohesion predicts children's comprehension overall [@pickrenContributionTextCharacteristics2022], and text properties bear differently on surface and inferential questions [@aparicioComprehensionPerformancesExplanatory2022].

*C2: narration and comprehension.* Its condition is that item-level comprehension responses exist and that accounts are observed both with and without narration. We would predict that, within an account, narration is positively associated with response correctness after adjustment for text, age band, reading level, accumulated reading and language. The expected size is small [@clintonlisellDoesReadingWhile2023; @woodUseTexttoSpeech2018], and the coefficient identifies an association, not an effect.

*C3: reading pace and comprehension.* It has the same condition as C2 and is restricted to sessions without narration. We would predict that an account's mean log reading time per word is negatively associated with response correctness, so that accounts with a faster habitual pace answer more accurately [@sortkaerBothSidesStory2021]. The within-account deviation term in the same model separates this between-account association from slow reading in a difficult or interrupted session.

*C4: machine-generated and human-authored text.* Its condition is that the classic stories are confirmed to be fixed, human-authored texts, identical for all users within a language. We would predict that the three text components have coefficients of the same sign for reading pace in generated and classic texts. Each component's interaction with the generated-or-classic indicator is predicted to be practically equivalent to zero. The hypothesis tests whether the two kinds of text are exchangeable. The closest evidence is the adult eye-movement corpus on machine-generated text [@bolligerEMTeCCorpusEye2025]. A practically non-negligible interaction would mean that a text property relates differently to children's reading pace in generated and human-authored stories.

## Timeline

The extract is built and held before submission, so its transfer is expected within four weeks of in-principle acceptance. Feature extraction and its hand-checked validation need only the story texts already received, and they will start on the day in-principle acceptance is confirmed, once Stage 1 review has fixed the feature set. The audit of the frozen extract and the outcome-blind dimension reduction will follow within three months of transfer, since the reduction depends on which texts have eligible readings. The confirmatory and sensitivity models will be fitted within a further four months. The Stage 2 manuscript will be submitted within twelve months of in-principle acceptance. [The author to confirm or adjust these intervals.] Any extension would be negotiated with the handling editor.

# Data availability

The data controller holds the session-level extract. It will be transferred to us only after the journal confirms in-principle acceptance, under a data-sharing agreement between the University of Oxford and the data controller. The English story texts are already public, in the `preregistration/story_texts` directory of the repository named under Code availability, under a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence agreed with their rights holders, Ferrero International and Gameloft. The texts in the other languages will be added there as they are delivered. On acceptance of the Stage 2 manuscript, we will deposit the computed text features, component scores and fitted model objects in [the named public repository, with a digital object identifier], with the story texts as analysed. The deposit will include the participant-flow counts, the laboratory log (a dated record of every analysis step and protocol deviation) and every table and figure underlying the reported results. Session-level fields that the agreement classes as commercially sensitive may be restricted. For each such field, we will state the reason and deposit a derived form sufficient to reproduce every reported analysis. Researchers will be able to request the restricted fields through [the named data controller contact or the mechanism the agreement specifies].

The manifest and the provider-computed counts contain no record of any individual and will be deposited in the same repository on receipt, before in-principle acceptance. The 35-row structural sample described under Pilot data is deposited there for peer review, under embargo until Stage 2 acceptance, with a view-only link for the editors.

# Code availability

All analysis code is version-controlled at <https://github.com/pablobernabeu/InTRACt_Interplay_of_Text_Reader_And_Context>, in the `preregistration` directory, which will be public and available for peer review at submission, with all Stage 1 materials in place. The directory contains the theory object with its checks and derived diagram, and the design specifications with the precision analysis, its recomputations at 0.95 assurance and under the Bayes-factor criterion, and its re-derivation at other shares of variance between texts. It also contains the scripts and record of the literature search, both versions of the count script supplied to the data controller, the scripts that extract and publish the story texts, and the frozen rules of the prior-derivation pipeline. The theory object, the design analysis and the literature search can be reproduced from these files now. Before the extract is transferred, we will add the prior-derivation script and the prior table it writes, both described under Priors, and the outcome-model code described under Randomisation and blinding. The frozen feature inventory will be added before any feature is linked to outcome data.

The four packages the protocol relies on are cited by their version-independent identifiers. The releases in use are theoryforge 0.6.0 [@bernabeuTheoryforge2026], pilotr 0.3.0 [@bernabeuPilotr2026], scopusflow 0.4.0 [@bernabeuScopusflow2026] and depictr 0.3.0 [@bernabeuDepictr2026]. The software versions behind the reported numbers are recorded with their outputs, in `design_analysis/session_info.txt`, `design_analysis/session_info_ordinal.txt` and `design_analysis/session_info_variance_sensitivity.txt` for the design analysis, `theory/tf_check.txt` for the theory object and `literature/scopus_run_stamp.txt` for the literature search. The design-analysis figures were composed with depictr, which checks each panel's type size and greyscale legibility at the journal's print width and refuses to save a panel that fails.
